audits.lens: micro1 engineer scoring ONLY the 30-point "Agent Solution & Engineering" row (tie-break #1). I am reading for two things the row names: "uses agents purposefully" (the self-check: which design choices helped the agent solve the problem?) and "is technically sound." I evaluate agents commercially, so I have a calibrated prior on which design moves are novel and which are Tuesday.
audits.why:
TECHNICALLY SOUND is where this is exceptional; USES AGENTS PURPOSEFULLY is where it is thin — and the row's own self-check question weights the second.

AS SPECIFIED IN §7 — 21/30.
Credit, and it is real: three capabilities each nailed to an observed failure; a custom tool with a typed return contract ({found, level, designation_exists, siblings, char_offset}) and three normalisation levels rather than a grep wrapper; GOOD.md committed before A1 exists; a headroom gate with genuine branch rules; guard metrics with pre-set numbers (false-defect ≤ 0.25); an attributor-completeness gate that blocks the headline; a pre-registered removed experiment with a directional leakage prediction (§7.8). Top-decile discipline; almost nobody in a ~100-entry field matches it. Deductions, largest first:

(a) The agent emits ONE BIT per item. Every design choice is therefore invisible except through an average. The row asks which choices helped; the only answer a judge can read off the artifact is "we handed it the document."
(b) The headline capability is CONTEXT. "RAG lifts a QA-shaped metric" is the single most-seen result in agent evaluation. 0.50 → 0.82 with the point-in-time text is a good measurement of a *task*; it is not a demonstration of *agent design*. And the honest version of the spec already concedes this — §7.3 explicitly says the 0.818 belongs to B0-agent, the BASELINE, not to the advanced solution. So the project's most impressive number is scored in the baseline row, not this one.
(c) Two of three capabilities are speculative at spec time. §7.4 pre-registers that the memory "may be promoted to the removed experiment." A purposefulness row cannot award full marks to a maybe.
(d) The evidence FOR THIS ROW is the ablation table, and at n = 84 it will be statistically empty. A 6 pp per-capability delta with ~12 discordant pairs split 9/3 gives McNemar exact p = 0.146. Three changelog rows reading "+6 pp, p ≈ 0.3" do not establish that any design choice helped. The 30-point row and the 15-point Measured Improvement row share one evidence base, and that base is underpowered by construction.
(e) anchor_resolve is a point-in-time fetch plus a three-level substring match — context wearing tool clothing. SKILL.md is a procedure in a file. Neither is wrong; neither is a choice a reader will remember an hour later.

WITH THE SEQUENCE/LEDGER REFRAME — 24/30. The +3 is real, for two reasons.
First, it converts memory from capability 3 into the thesis, and the memory/consistency trap is the one appendix technique the field skipped (1 of 64 visible entries). "Each instruction is individually valid and the rule is collectively defective" is Appendix Example 3's own sentence — "each sentence can be correct while the series as a whole no longer feels coherent" — transposed into a domain with mechanical ground truth. Judges handed that technique out for free and nobody took it.
Second, the agent stops being a classifier. It carries a world model forward, and "retrieval structurally cannot simulate an ordered edit sequence" is a mechanism-level, quotable claim rather than a capability-menu label.

Why it stops at 24 and not 27:
(a) The output is still one bit. The invisibility problem is untouched.
(b) THE COLLISION CLASS SIZE IS UNMEASURED. Nothing in the kill test counts it — §7.7 names it as the hard case and gives no n. This project already made this exact error once and caught it: 103 alleged splits audited down to 13 genuine from 6 documents, with the lesson written down ("audit any mechanically-derived positive class before believing its size"). Putting the 30-point row on an uncounted class is the same bet, taken again, one file later.
(c) The reframe opens a NEW trivial-solution attack that has not been run: a purely syntactic AMDPAR simulator over (operation, designation) tuples with no CFR text at all — flag two operations on one designation, an "add" onto an existing designation, or a redesignate followed by any later operation inside the redesignated range. That is ~60 lines. The nearest measured analogue is on the contestant's side (the ~150-line anchor + paragraph-hierarchy script scored 0.5855 vs a 0.5000 constant), but it was measured on the anchor task, not on collisions. Until that script is run, the reframe's foreclosure is asserted.
(d) The ledger's ablation is now the headline and will be measured on a subclass of perhaps 10–25 items. Two unpowered claims stacked is worse than one.
(e) The premise that OFR executes instructions sequentially against each other's OUTPUT (rather than each against the pre-rule text) is asserted in §7.4 as "the actual OFR execution model" with no citation. It is almost certainly right — the Document Drafting Handbook orders redesignations before amendments to redesignated material precisely because they compose, and NARA's note wording "a PORTION of the amendment could not be incorporated" implies partial execution — but it is load-bearing for the entire reframe and must be cited, not claimed.
audits.what_a_27_of_30_looks_like:
Four moves. The first two are the ones that actually buy the points; the last two are cheap and are what I have never seen.

1. THE UNIT OF PREDICTION MOVES FROM (rule, section) TO (rule, section, instruction), AND THE OUTPUT IS THE LEDGER, NOT THE LABEL.
The agent emits a per-instruction execution trace: operation, anchor, resolution level (exact / whitespace-collapsed / alphanumeric), the designation set before and after, and for a failure the exact reason plus the character offset where the quoted anchor diverges. WILL_FAIL becomes a derived field of that trace, not the artifact. Two consequences, both decisive for this row:
   • Every capability becomes directly readable in the output. A judge scrolls one worksheet row and SEES anchor_resolve return {found:false, level:none, siblings:[(b)(1),(b)(2)]} and SEES the ledger record "(b)(4) → (b)(5) after instruction 5, so instruction 12's target no longer exists." No inference from an average required. That is literally the row's question answered on the page.
   • n multiplies by ~4.5 (defective sections average 4.93 instructions). 84 items becomes ~380 instruction-level judgements; clustered by FR document the effective n is maybe 180–220. The same 6 pp delta that gave McNemar p = 0.146 at 12 discordant pairs gives p ≈ 0.08 at 40 discordant (26/14) and p ≈ 0.018 at 28/12. Per-capability contribution moves from "never significant" to "sometimes significant." This is the ONLY route by which the evidence for the 30-point row becomes statistically legible inside the available pool.

2. PER-INSTRUCTION GROUND TRUTH, DERIVED MECHANICALLY, STILL ZERO AUTHORED.
Diff the point-in-time CFR section at (effective_date − 1 day) against (effective_date + grace), restricted to sections amended by exactly one rule in that window. The diff tells you which operations landed and which did not — per instruction, from NARA's own codified product. Note the distinction §7.8 nearly obscures: the post-effective text must be withheld from the AGENT (it leaks the label — correctly identified as the removed experiment) but using it to BUILD labels is exactly what a freeze boundary is for. Property 1 survives intact.
Chance falls from 0.50 to ~1/k ≈ 0.20–0.25, and — this is the part that matters for the trivial-solution test — always-WILL_FAIL scores 0.500 on the binary metric and ≈ 0.00 on this one. The degenerate policy is killed by the shape of the output space rather than by count-matching.

3. THE VERIFICATION IS EXECUTABLE, NOT ARGUMENTATIVE.
Ship apply_instruction(section_tree, operation, anchor, designation) → new_tree | Failure(reason). The agent does not assert "this executes"; the harness EXECUTES it. The agent's WILL_EXECUTE is accepted only if the simulated edit succeeds and its WILL_FAIL only if the simulated edit throws for the reason the agent named. You do not need the full AMDPAR vocabulary — only the operations present in your 42–84 items — and as a checker over designations plus a substring match rather than a full XML editor it is ~300–400 lines and 4–6 hours. This is the opposite of the thing micro1's CEO calls circular: no model in the scoring path, and the agent can no longer be right for the wrong reason.

4. A REPAIR METRIC. repair@1.
For every predicted defect the agent emits a corrected amendatory instruction, and the harness re-runs apply_instruction on it. Score the fraction whose correction executes cleanly. This is a second, fully deterministic metric that no constant can win, that no baseline can fake, and that is the thing the actual user needs — the drafter's next action is writing a correcting document, which costs another Federal Register cycle. An agent whose success criterion is that a deterministic downstream process ACCEPTS ITS OUTPUT is the shape I essentially never see in submissions, and it is exactly micro1's own published triad: reproducible environment, deterministic verification, golden reference solution.

Two cheap additions that finish the row:
5. An ABSTAIN class routed to the one named human checkpoint (the unresolved collision), with accuracy-at-coverage published. Zero of 64 visible entries do abstention.
6. Report each capability's ablation on THE SUBCLASS IT WAS BUILT FOR — the tool on missing-anchor instructions, the skill on multi-instruction sections, the ledger on the collision subclass — with the whole-set average printed beside it and explicitly named as the misleading number. That is the project's own hot take ("measure which class got better, because the average will lie to you") applied to its own ablations, which is the strongest possible internal consistency a submission can have.
audits.biggest_weakness:
The agent's output is one bit, and that single fact causes every other deduction on this row.

Because the output is a label, no design choice can be seen doing work — it can only be inferred from a delta in an average. And because the unit of prediction is (rule, section), the pool caps at n = 84, so those deltas are structurally too small to establish anything: 6 pp with ~12 discordant pairs is McNemar p = 0.146. The 30-point row is scored on "which design choices helped the agent," and the submission's answer will be three changelog rows that each say "+6 pp, not significant," attached to a headline gain (0.50 → 0.82) that §7.3 itself correctly assigns to the BASELINE arm, not to the advanced solution.

So the project's most impressive number is not this row's number, and this row's numbers will not be establishable. That is how a submission with genuinely top-decile engineering discipline lands at 21 instead of 27.

The second-largest weakness, and the one that could be fatal rather than merely costly: the sequence/collision class has never been counted. It is the reframe's entire load-bearing structure and its n is unknown. This document has already audited one mechanically-derived positive class from 103 down to 13 and written the lesson down; the reframe asks the reader to trust an uncounted class again.
audits.recommendation:
ADOPT THE REFRAME, BUT NOT ALONE. Sequence is the right thesis and the wrong stopping point: it fixes purposefulness and leaves the output a bit. Take the reframe AND move the unit of prediction to the instruction. Gate both on a census you can run before writing any agent code.

FIRST 90 MINUTES — the collision census, run as measurement AND as attack. No model calls.
1. Pull the ~92 editorial-note sections; resolve each to its FR document; attribute AMDPARs. Print the histogram of k = instructions per section. GATE: if median k ≤ 2 the sequence thesis is dead on arrival — there is nothing to sequence — and the ledger stays capability 3 exactly as §7.4 specifies.
2. Count sections where ≥2 instructions touch the same paragraph designation, or a redesignate is followed by any later operation inside its range. That is the collision-class size. ~60 lines. GATE: if the count is < 8, the reframe is an anecdote, not a centrepiece.
3. RUN THAT SAME 60-LINE SCRIPT AS THE TRIVIAL-SOLUTION ATTACK on the count-matched pairs — a purely syntactic AMDPAR simulator with no CFR text. GATE: if it clears ~0.70, the reframe dies by hard constraint 4 and you must know that before H6, not after H15. (Prior is favourable: the ~150-line anchor + hierarchy script scored 0.5855 against a 0.5000 constant. But it was measured on anchors, not collisions.)
4. Twenty minutes with the Document Drafting Handbook to CITE sequential execution rather than assert it, and to check whether any editorial-note text names the defective instruction (free localisation labels if so).

THEN, IN PRIORITY ORDER, INSIDE 24 HOURS:
• Fix the AMDPAR attributor to ≥ 0.90 first. §8.2 is right that this is the highest-value task, and now it is also the prerequisite for instruction-level scoring — a truncated block means you cannot score instructions at all. Non-negotiable, H1–H4.
• Build apply_instruction as a designation-state checker (not a full XML editor), covering only the operation vocabulary your pool actually contains. ~4–6 h. This one component simultaneously delivers the ledger, the executable verification, and repair@1.
• Derive per-instruction labels by diffing (effective_date − 1) against (effective_date + grace) on sections amended by exactly one rule in the window. ~2–3 h. Risk: multi-rule sections and OFR editorial cleanup add diff noise — filter mechanically and publish the exclusion count.
• Keep the binary (rule, section) accuracy as a REPORTED metric — it is pre-registered, safe, and comparable to the pilot — but make instruction-level localisation the primary, with the binary printed beside it as the coarse view. If the diff-labels come out dirty, demote localisation and repair@1 to secondary metrics with the derivation stated; you still gain most of the row's points because the LEDGER ARTIFACT is what makes the design choices visible, independent of which number is headline.
• Report each capability's ablation on its own target subclass with the whole-set average beside it, explicitly labelled as the misleading number — your own hot take, applied to your own results.

WHAT I WOULD CUT TO PAY FOR IT: the pre-2017 govinfo fallback (§8.3). It buys pool size for a metric you are replacing with one that multiplies n by 4.5 anyway. Ship 2017+ only, state the coverage boundary, and spend those hours on apply_instruction.

WHAT NOT TO DO: do not lead the README or the video with "the agent scores 0.82 because we gave it the CFR text." That is the baseline arm's number, it is the most-seen result in this business, and it is the framing that caps this row at 21. Lead with the rule that was defective as a whole while every instruction in it was individually valid, and show the ledger localising the step where the two collided.

audits.lens: Agent architecture — what design patterns actually earn the 30-point "Agent Solution & Engineering" row, judged by an agent-evaluation company; then where this project lands on that taxonomy. I ran the reframe's central claim against real Federal Register data before scoring it.
audits.why:
FIRST PRINCIPLES, IGNORING THE PROJECT.

The row's self-check is "Which design choices HELPED the agent solve the problem?" — a causal-attribution question, not an inventory question. So a capability earns in proportion to how structurally impossible the task is without it, not how impressive it looks. Five tiers:

- T0 Decorative (earns <=0): persona fan-out, critic layers with no external referent (a critic without a tool is a second sample), planners nobody reads, memory-as-cache, orchestration that is a for-loop. micro1 has published that over-produced traces score LOWEST ("10-20 tool calls, repeated planning loops - frequently the lowest-scoring"). Also: a critic agent grading the worker agent is the CEO's chicken-and-egg objection re-run inside one submission.
- T1 Efficiency: caching, retries, format constraints. Answer to "what helped" = "it got faster."
- T2 Accuracy-shifting: retrieval/context. Legitimate, named in the PDF, but it has the largest gap in the whole menu between measured gain and engineering credit, because the mechanism is obvious, the implementation is 30 lines, and the judges will have read ~100 of them this weekend. "We gave the agent the document" is a true sentence that buys few of the 30 points.
- T3 Enabling (where the points live). Three sub-patterns: (3a) state-carrying simulation - the answer depends on operations applied in order, so a stateless call cannot REPRESENT the task, not merely do it worse; (3b) ground-truth-establishing tool - a deterministic tool returning a fact the model can neither generate nor check by reasoning (exact string presence, parser result, formula), where the tool output is independently checkable by the judge; (3c) scored restraint/abstention with ONE named human checkpoint at ONE failure mode (their Chief Economist: human expertise "at the failure modes that genuinely require it, not spread thin").
- T4 Architectural necessity: a class of wrong answer made impossible by construction, not detected. This is Chinmoy's own signature ("the model structurally cannot state an unbacked price") and it is the only claim in a submission that survives adversarial reading without a p-value. micro1 sells verifiers; a verifier that forecloses beats one that detects.

Two structural points that matter more than the tier list. (1) The deliverable for this row is the ABLATION MATRIX plus the per-failure-class delta, not the capability list - micro1's doctrine is "completion is a first-class result", "no hand-picked keys", per-class reporting. (2) micro1's own published rubric design is DECOMPOSITION (RealmLegal IRAC: issue 4% / rule 33% / application 48% / conclusion 9%). A submission that decomposes its primary judgement into named, weighted, separately-scored sub-skills is speaking their dialect - and it also buys statistical power for free, which is this project's binding constraint.

NOW THE PROJECT — AND I MEASURED THE REFRAME BEFORE SCORING IT.

I pulled full_text_xml for all 36 FR rules behind the existing 82-item pilot pool (Federal Register API, cached at .../scratchpad/fr/*.xml) and parsed 5,590 AMDPAR elements into 1,810 distinct (doc, section) targets. The reframe's headline mechanism — "instruction 12 deletes a paragraph instruction 5 already redesignated" — does not survive contact with the corpus:

- 0 of 82 harvested instruction blocks contain the string "redesignat". 0 of the 68 labelled pool items I could match to AMDPARs has a redesignation instruction. Two independent extraction paths agree.
- Only 2 of 68 labelled pool items have >=2 separate AMDPAR elements targeting the same section at all. The sequencing precondition is absent from the LABELLED population, which is the only population that has ground truth.
- Across all 1,810 (doc, section) targets: 64 (3.5%) have >=2 AMDPARs, 40 have a redesignation, and only 13 (0.7%) have both — the structural precondition for a collision.
- Of those 13, a 15-line detector I wrote (designations touched by a redesignation AMDPAR intersected with designations touched by any other AMDPAR for that section) fires on exactly 1. Collision detection over parsed triples IS a script. It is the most script-able part of the entire task.
- Worse: 95 of 5,590 AMDPARs (1.7%) mention redesignation, and 37 of those 95 (39%) contain the literal phrase "newly redesignated". OFR's house style ANNOUNCES the cross-instruction dependency in prose. A one-line regex finds it. The single fired case reads verbatim: "37. Amend newly redesignated § 125.18 by revising paragraph (b)".

This is CROSSCheck's split case repeating exactly: a named hard case with n=0 after the eval set's own construction, and the "103 splits -> 13 genuine" correction is the same shape. §7.7 asserts the intra-rule collision is the hard case and is the one claim in a 934-line document with no count attached. That absence was the tell.

Three more numbers from the same pass, all pointing the same direction: 65 of 82 harvested blocks are under 200 chars (median 88.5) — truncated lead-ins; 40 of 82 have empty point-in-time section text (the pre-2017 versioner gap); and only 6 of 82 have BOTH a full block and section text. The pilot's honest usable n is 6, not 11.

SCORING AS SPECIFIED (21/30). Structure is right and above the field: three capabilities each derived from a numbered failure class, a genuinely T3b deterministic tool, SKILL.md shipped as a file (their RedlineBench layout), pre-registered thresholds with McNemar, symmetric guard metrics, a compute-matched control, and a removed experiment with a pre-registered DIRECTIONAL prediction (current-text leakage) — that last one is rare and excellent. What caps it: §7.3 concedes the +27pp headline belongs to B0-agent, a sanctioned baseline type 2. The agent-attributable residual is a pre-registered +8pp on n=84, unmeasured even in pilot. The output is one bit, so no capability can be attributed to output structure. The capabilities are sequentially dependent (skill calls tool; ledger is populated by the skill's parse), so the ablation is a chain, not a matrix — and a chain cannot separate the tool's contribution from the skill's when they are always co-present. And §7.4 pre-emptively hedges the one T3a capability as possibly-removable, which caps the ceiling by design.

SCORING THE REFRAME AS PROPOSED (19/30 — it goes DOWN). It moves the thesis from T2 to T3a, which is the right DIRECTION and the highest-earning pattern available. But as literally proposed it trades a modest true claim for a striking unevidenced one, and the gap is discoverable by any judge with the same public API I just used, in about ten minutes. A centrepiece with n<=2 in the labelled pool, defeated by a 15-line detector on the general case, and self-announced in prose 39% of the time, is not a thesis — it is an overclaim that contaminates the credibility of the true findings around it. It also introduces a live kill risk the existing foreclosure does not cover: the 26-feature permutation null (best 0.5934, p=0.185) was over CHEAP features. A structural feature "section has a redesignation AMDPAR plus an overlapping-designation AMDPAR" has never been tested against that null. Building the thesis on an untested 20-line attack is how the previous front-runner died.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY AGENT-HARD HERE, which the spec treats as infrastructure. Median AMDPAR is 81 chars. OFR fragments one logical instruction across a lead-in element, lettered sub-elements, and quoted anchors that spill into adjacent elements — the 2016-18075 item literally splits as "13. Amend §§ 766.102 and 766.112 by removing the words..." / "a. § 766.102(b)(3)(ii); and". Reassembling fragmented, ambiguous, sometimes internally defective prose into (operation, anchor, designation) triples is the part no script does reliably — the kill test's own attributor failed on 13 of 24 items and the independent harvest dropped 25 of 86, both non-randomly and correlated with the label. That is not a harvest bug to be fixed before scoring. It is the task. The spec's H4 gate ("attributor completeness >= 0.90 before any headline number") is quietly outsourcing the agent's hardest job to a preprocessing script and then measuring what is left.
audits.what_a_27_of_30_looks_like:
Ten concrete properties. The first three are the ones that move it from 21 to 27.

1. THE OUTPUT IS AN ARTIFACT, NOT A BIT. The agent emits a codification worksheet: one row per instruction — operation, anchor as quoted, target designation, resolved yes/no, at which normalisation level (exact / whitespace-collapsed / alphanumeric), char offset, and state-after. WILL_FAIL is a DERIVED field, not the product. The §7.10 plan already builds this at H20-22 and calls it presentation. It should be the output. A structured output is what lets a capability be attributed to a PART of the answer.

2. THREE METRICS AT THREE GRANULARITIES FROM ONE CASE SET — this is how the n=84 power problem is solved without more data, and it mirrors micro1's own IRAC decomposition:
   (a) PRIMARY, section-level bit vs the NARA editorial note, n=84, string equality, no model.
   (b) DIAGNOSTIC, instruction-level anchor-claim correctness vs a DETERMINISTIC oracle ("is this quoted string present in the point-in-time text at this designation?" is a computable fact, not a judgement, so it costs zero authored labels). 42 pairs x ~4.4 instructions ≈ 185 records. This is where the tool's contribution gets statistical power. It cannot be the primary metric — a script trivially scores 1.0 because it IS the script — but as a diagnostic it is perfect.
   (c) HARD-CASE PARTITION score, per class.

3. THE HALLUCINATION RATE. From (2b): "Without anchor_resolve, the agent asserted a quoted anchor was present in the section when it was not, in X% of instructions; with the tool, 0% by construction." One sentence, one number, and it converts "we added a tool" into "we measured the failure class the tool forecloses" — a T4 claim, not a T2 one. This is the single best sentence available to this submission for this row, and it is nearly free.

4. THE POOL IS PARTITIONED BY MECHANISM BEFORE ANY ARM RUNS, and the partition is published as code: single-instruction / multi-instruction-independent / multi-instruction-interacting / fragmented-across-elements. Every arm reports per-partition. A capability's claim is then evidenced by a partition shape (~0 on partitions where it cannot bite, large where it can) rather than by a p-value on n=84.

5. THE ABLATION IS HONEST ABOUT ITS CHAIN. Say outright that skill-without-tool and ledger-without-skill are undefined, present the chain, and then cross ONE genuinely independent axis against it (e.g. tool x ledger with skill fixed) so at least one real interaction cell exists. A fake 2^3 matrix over dependent capabilities looks rigorous to a generalist and reads as sloppy to these judges.

6. ONE CAPABILITY MEASURED AT ZERO AND KEPT IN THE REPORT. Given the measurements above the ledger is the likely candidate; the honest move is to ship two capabilities and publish the ledger as the removed experiment with its n=0 collision count as the reason.

7. ONE NAMED HUMAN CHECKPOINT AT ONE FAILURE MODE, rendered as a real element of the worksheet (unresolved anchor: both readings, the paragraph trace, a decision field) — not a sentence in the README.

8. TOKENS AND COST PER ARM in the same table as accuracy, with the compute-matched B0' control, so the judge can see the capability was not just more compute.

9. A TRAJECTORY WHERE THE PLAN CHANGES. One trace: anchor_resolve returns not-found at exact, found at whitespace-collapsed, and the agent revises WILL_FAIL to WILL_EXECUTE with reasoning visible. That is the artifact micro1 buys at $2-15 a trace and the proof the capability was load-bearing at runtime, not only in aggregate.

10. AGENT INSTRUCTIONS SHIPPED AS FILES (SKILL.md + per-task instruction.md), because the PDF requires it and it is literally their RedlineBench layout.
audits.biggest_weakness:
The design's own headline improvement is attributed to the sanctioned baseline, not to the agent architecture — so the 30-point row is being asked to run on an +8pp residual that has never been measured, not even in pilot. §7.3 says it plainly: "This is the bar A1 must clear... do not present 0.818 as the advanced solution's achievement." A judge who reads that honest sentence applies exactly that discount to this row.

The mechanism that caps it is the one-bit output. Any capability, however well-chosen, ultimately moves one bit on n=84, so nothing can be attributed to output structure and per-class reporting splits the set into cells of ~20. The reframe is an attempt to escape that cap by changing the STORY; it does not work, because the cap is in the output shape, not the narrative. Change the output shape and the cap lifts — the same case set then yields ~185 instruction-level records and a deterministic diagnostic oracle at no labelling cost.

Second-order but urgent: the spec treats AMDPAR reassembly as preprocessing to be fixed to >=0.90 completeness before scoring. Median AMDPAR is 81 characters and OFR splits one logical instruction across a lead-in, lettered sub-elements, and spilled quoted anchors. That reassembly is the only part of this task a script genuinely cannot do — it is the agent's job description, and the plan gives it away to a regex.
audits.recommendation:
Keep the project. Kill the reframe as proposed. Change the output shape instead.

The project is sound: clean licence (17 U.S.C. §105, no key, no robots restriction), a real user with a public exposure, a measured foreclosure (best cheap feature 0.5934 sitting inside its own permutation null at p=0.185), a deterministic scorer, and the most legible 60-second demo in the search. With ~47 hours left, abandoning is strictly worse. But the sequence/ledger centrepiece must not ship as the thesis — 0 redesignations in 68 labelled items, 13 of 1,810 (0.7%) targets with the precondition corpus-wide, 1 of 13 detected by a 15-line script, and 39% of redesignation instructions announcing the dependency in the phrase "newly redesignated".

DO THIS INSTEAD, in order.

H0-2 (three gates, all cheap, all decisive — run before writing any capability):
- G1 COLLISION COUNT. Re-run my measurement on the full harvest once the pool is rebuilt. Gate: >=10 items with a genuine cross-instruction dependency, >=4 on the defective side. My prior from the 36-rule sample is that you will get 0-2. If so, the ledger becomes capability 3 with an honest small-n caveat, or the removed experiment — and you find that out in hour two instead of hour seventeen.
- G2 THE STRUCTURAL-FEATURE ATTACK. Add "has a redesignation AMDPAR whose designations intersect another AMDPAR's" plus "count of distinct designations touched" to the 26-feature sweep and re-run the SAME permutation null. Gate: must land inside the null. This is the one attack the existing foreclosure does not cover, and the reframe would have made it the headline.
- G3 ANCHOR TYPOLOGY. Count what fraction of pool instructions carry a quoted anchor at all. Across 5,590 corpus AMDPARs it is 47.8%; in my crude pool matching it fell to 19%. If the pool's anchors are that sparse, anchor_resolve is decorative and you need to know before H9.

Then reshape rather than rebuild:
1. Make the codification worksheet the agent's OUTPUT (move it from H20-22 to H7). WILL_FAIL becomes a derived field.
2. Add the instruction-level deterministic oracle and report anchor-claim accuracy at n~185 per arm. Zero authored labels; it is a computable fact. This is the fix for the power problem and it makes the tool's contribution provable rather than inferable.
3. Lead the 30-point row with the HALLUCINATION RATE, not the accuracy delta. "The agent asserted a quoted anchor was present when it was not, in X% of instructions without the tool; 0% with it, by construction" is a T4 foreclosure claim and it is Chinmoy's own signature move, which is why he will write it convincingly.
4. Reframe the AGENT's job honestly as reassembling fragmented, ambiguous, sometimes self-defective amendatory prose into executable triples — the part the attributor failed at in 13 of 24 items and the independent harvest failed at in 25 of 86. That is the genuine seam, it is not scriptable, and it happens to be exactly what the existing evidence already documents.
5. Keep the ledger, demoted, as a STATE COLUMN in the worksheet rather than a claim. If G1 comes back at n<=2, publish it as the removed experiment with the collision count as the stated reason. A removed capability with a measured n=0 hard-case class is worth more on this row than a kept capability with an unmeasured one — and it is a far better story than the reframe would have been.

A ledger is not needed to read two adjacent lines. So the ledger ablation will most likely land at ~0, which is exactly the outcome §7.4 fears, and the reframe would have made it the centrepiece.

ALT-1 — "CODIFY IT": THE AGENT EXECUTES THE RULE INSTEAD OF PREDICTING A LABEL. TRIVIAL-SOLUTION PROFILE, MEASURED OVER 6,169 SURGICAL/STRUCTURAL INSTRUCTIONS: 32.3% are purely mechanical quoted replaces a find-and-replace script does outright; 22.0% carry a judgement anchor (wherever-it-appears 5.3%, table entries 5.2%, definition scope 4.6%, sentence position 4.1%, alphabetical placement 3.2%, headings 2.2%); 5.0% are both. WHY IT SCORES ON THE 30-POINT ROW: state-carrying is the MECHANISM of every item, not a rare defect class, so the ledger ablation is "execute in document order vs. execute each instruction independently against the original text" — an ablation that is guaranteed to fire on the 38% of rules where one section receives >=2 instructions, and catastrophically on the 5.8% redesignate-then-add rules. Verification becomes a deterministic post-execution assertion (every removed anchor absent, every added anchor present) with a directly measurable delta. ONE TRAP I HAVE TO NAME AGAINST MY OWN PROPOSAL: do NOT make the per-instruction metric an executed/blocked bit. Most instructions execute, so always-EXECUTED would score ~0.95 and filter 4 kills it. The scored unit must be the CONTENT — (removed span, added span, designation) matched against OFR's codified text — where there is no constant to hide behind.

audits.what_a_27_of_30_looks_like:
A 27+/30 submission on this row satisfies four things a judge can check in ninety seconds, none of which the incumbent currently does:

1. THE AGENT'S OUTPUT IS THE ARTIFACT THE USER NEEDS, AND THE METRIC SCORES THAT ARTIFACT. Not a WILL_FAIL/WILL_EXECUTE bit with an unscored HTML worksheet beside it. The drafter does not want a probability that her rule breaks; she wants the codified text her rule produces and the instruction number that will not run. The primary metric must be the fidelity of that document, per instruction, against OFR's own codification — so that improving the agent and improving the deliverable are the same act.

2. AT LEAST ONE CAPABILITY IS STRUCTURALLY NECESSARY, WITH AN ABLATION WHOSE OUTCOME YOU CAN PREDICT AND WHICH ACTUALLY FIRES. The test: can you name a run configuration that removes the capability and makes the number collapse for a stated mechanical reason? For the ledger that configuration is "execute the rule's instructions independently against the original text instead of in document order" — and it fires on 38% of rules (>=2 instructions to one section) and destroys the 5.8% redesignate-then-add rules outright. Compare the incumbent, where the ledger's ablation is a delta on a binary label at n=84 and §7.4 already pre-concedes it may be zero.

3. THE HEADLINE GAIN BELONGS TO THE SOLUTION, NOT TO THE BASELINE. Right now the honest reading of §7.3 is "the big number is what happens when you put the document in the prompt, and the solution is worth eight more points." A 27+ submission's headline delta is produced by a design choice — ordering, state, a normalisation ladder, a post-hoc assertion — and the retrieval gain is reported as the baseline it is.

4. THE TRAJECTORY SHOWS PLAN -> EXECUTE -> VERIFY -> REPAIR, NOT FETCH -> GREP -> DECIDE. micro1 buys agent traces commercially at $2-15 each and warns that over-produced traces score worst; the target is a trace with SHAPE, not length. Executing eleven instructions in order, hitting an anchor that does not resolve at exact match, escalating to whitespace-collapsed, finding it, recording the state change, and then at instruction nine discovering the designation it needs was renumbered at instruction four — that is a legible mechanism. Two lookups and a verdict is not.

Concretely, the results table of a 27+ entry has these rows on ONE case set: one-prompt-no-text; one-prompt-with-text; the find-and-replace script (with its honest CV ceiling); agent with tool only; + ledger; + verification; and a compute-matched control — with per-instruction-type breakdown (mechanical replace / definition scope / sentence position / alphabetical / redesignation) so the changelog can say WHICH class each iteration fixed. That per-class table is what turns "we added memory" into "memory bought +N points and all of it came from the redesignation class, here are the eleven items."

Measure the drift/structural split first — one 20-line script, one hour — and if drift is >80%, drop repair to a UI affordance and claim nothing.

(3) The pitch's flagship case class is a minority. 26 of those 33 labelled items contain zero extractable quoted anchor. Population-wide, only 1,019 of 1,984 (rule,section) items (51.4%) contain any quoted string at all. The video line - "remove the words 'and safety' from paragraph (b)(3); those words are not there" - describes ~21% of the labelled pool and ~half the population. The other failures are designation/hierarchy failures, which are far less legible.

(4) eCFR is a hostile harvest target and section 7.10 budgets it at 3 hours. Measured: HTTP 429 at any concurrency above ~4, HTTP 503 "This website is under heavy load (queue full)" even serially, and 502s. First parallel pass returned usable text for 22 of 82 pilot items. A serial pass with backoff took the better part of an hour to reach 38. 24 of the 82 pilot items are pre-2017 and cannot be served by the versioner at all; govinfo annual editions are unimplemented.

(5) The user is small. The whole observable failure population is ~92 live editorial notes, 184 distinct sections from the pilot's single query phrase, 306 from the union of six phrasings I ran today. That is the entire universe of the problem.

(6) 143/143 died and 2 came back only after redesign, which is at least as much evidence that the search frame was wrong as that this candidate is right.

=== WHY THE CASE FAILS ANYWAY ===

Abandonment needs a destination and there isn't one. With ~24 build hours, ~8 owed to video/repro-guide/trajectories, a replacement must reach >=10 cases, a fair baseline, three evidenced iterations and survive the trivial-solution test, starting from zero. The measured base rate for surviving that test as generated is 2/143. The current project has a working harvest, a labelled pilot, a measured baseline table, a clean licence, and - decisively - a cheap honest abort at H6 that costs ~6 hours and answers the question at n=84. A new idea has no such gate; you find out at hour 20. That asymmetry settles it.

And two of the abandonment case's own premises died today:

- The attributor - which section 8 calls "the weak link" and section 7.10 calls "the single highest-value build task" - is a 20-line fix and I did it. Of 5,590 AMDPAR elements across 36 FR rules, 3,473 (62%) name no section because they are the lettered sub-instructions ("b. Remove the dollar amount ...") emitted as sibling AMDPAR elements after a lead-in. Carry the last-named section forward and unattributable AMDPARs drop to 46/5,590 = 0.8%. Completeness goes from 0.46 to 0.99. That is the single largest risk in the build plan, retired in an afternoon.
- Fixing it does NOT break property 3. Under the corrected count, positives average 3.38 instruction blocks vs 2.70 for negatives, but the best tuned-on-test threshold reaches only 0.5610 on the 82-item set - BELOW its own permutation null mean of 0.5701, empirical p = 0.61. The count-matching survives the attributor fix.
- Harvest cost collapses. Fetch at PART granularity, not section: one call to /versioner/v1/full/{date}/title-47.xml?part=25 returned 624,492 bytes containing 131 sections in 9.9s. A rule touches a handful of parts, so ~1,984 section fetches become ~100 part fetches. The rate-limit problem largely disappears.

=== NOW THE REFRAME YOU ASKED ME TO EVALUATE. IT IS A DOWNGRADE. ===

I measured its pool. Across 1,984 (rule,section) items from 36 rules, using the fixed attributor:
  items with >=2 instruction blocks:                                     833 (42.0%)
  items where a designation is touched again after redesignate/remove/add: 62 (3.12%)
  items that are genuinely ORDER-SENSITIVE (a redesignation is involved): 26 (1.31%)
In the pilot's own 82-item labelled gold set: 3 items have a collision. Two positive, one negative.

Worse, the modal ordering-sensitive pattern is correct drafting, not defect. 15 of the 26 are redesignate-then-add, e.g. 05-8447 section 75.6: "b. Redesignate paragraphs (a)(38) through (a)(41) as (a)(39) through (a)(42); c. Add new paragraphs (a)(38), (a)(43), and (a)(44)". That is the standard OFR idiom for inserting a paragraph. It appears in every well-drafted rule that inserts anything. And 29 of the 62 are remove-then-remove: two independent string substitutions in the same paragraph, not an interaction at all.

This is the CROSSCheck split-case failure repeating exactly. Section 1 of the kill test killed CROSSCheck partly because "the named hard case is excluded by the design's own filter... the hard case has n=0 in the benchmark that is built to showcase it," and section 5 corrected 103 alleged splits down to "thirteen rows from six documents." The ledger's hard case is 2 positive rows in the entire labelled pool. Promoting it to centrepiece repeats the mistake the kill test was written to catch.

And there is a deeper objection the pool size only makes concrete. "Simulate the edits in order and carry state forward" is a specification for a compiler. It is a state machine over a text buffer with a 300-line reference implementation. The reframe's premise - "retrieval structurally cannot do it" - is true and irrelevant, because retrieval is not the competitor; apply_edits(section_text, instruction_list) is. Divergent research's own law 3 says it: "if a task can be checked in 20 lines of model-free code, it can usually be solved in 200." Moving the headline from retrieval to sequence moves it INTO the trivial-solution blast radius, not out of it. When a judge asks "why does an agent carry this state rather than an interpreter?", there is no answer.

Third problem: the label unit forbids it. NARA's editorial note names a SECTION and an FR citation, never an instruction index - the kill test says so itself, which is why the prediction unit moved to (rule, section) in the first place. Each CFR section is an independent text buffer; there is no cross-section state to carry. The only genuine state is intra-section, and that is the 1.31%.

Scoring: as specified today the row is ~20/30 - three named capabilities each traced to a measured failure is the right shape and beats most of the field, but the honest answer to "which design choices helped the agent solve the problem?" is "we gave it the document," which is capability zero (it is B0-agent, the BASELINE, as section 7.3 concedes), capability 3 has a measured pool of 2 positives, and capability 1 measures at chance in my implementation. With the sequence reframe it drops to ~18: you spend build hours on the rarest class, you promote a deterministic simulation to your thesis, and you hand the judge the counter-question.

=== THE REFRAME THAT ACTUALLY WORKS: SCALE, NOT SEQUENCE ===

Same corpus, same NARA labels, same freeze. Move the unit of work from (rule, section) to THE WHOLE RULE, and make the deliverable the codification worksheet section 7.10 already schedules for H20-22: for every section this final rule amends, will it codify?

Measured on the 36 harvested rules:
  sections amended per rule: min 4, q1 12, median 28, q3 67, max 443, mean 55.1
  total decisions 1,984, known-defective 42, base rate 2.12%
  constant "flag everything":            recall 1.000, precision 0.0212, F1 0.0415
  constant "flag nothing":               F1 0.0000
  best tuned-on-test single-feature script over 10 cheap features (max paragraph depth >= 7): F1 0.1100, precision 0.070, recall 0.262
  next best (n_designations >= 10): F1 0.0862;  n_instructions >= 5: F1 0.0707

That is the strongest foreclosure anywhere in this project's history and it costs nothing to obtain. Compare the current design: it needs exact instruction-count matching, pre-registered as code, to force the constant to 0.5000, and even then the best feature reaches 0.5934 and has to be argued down with a permutation null. At rule level the script ceiling is 0.11 against a 0.04 floor - the base rate does the foreclosing, by construction, with no matching, no pairing, no exclusion ladder. The most fragile component of the entire design is deleted, not defended.

It also makes the agent architecture load-bearing instead of decorative, which is the whole point of the 30-point row:
- 443 sections in one rule with 2 defects. The agent cannot high-effort every section. Triage-then-escalate becomes a real design choice with a measurable cost-per-task, not a bolt-on. Orchestration earns its place instead of being claimed.
- Memory acquires a reason that survives the 1.31% finding: the running part structure (which paragraph designations exist after instructions 1..k) is needed to READ instruction k+1 correctly, on 42% of items, not to catch a collision on 1.31%.
- Verification acquires teeth: at a 2% base rate, the dominant failure is false alarms. The guard metric stops being a footnote and becomes the metric.
- The needle-in-haystack is the hard case, for free, and it is the best video in the search: 443 sections, one rule, "here are the two OFR could not codify."
- >=10 cases is 10 rules; you already have 36. n at the decision level is ~2,000, which is 24x the n=84 the current design is straining toward.

Two honest threats to it, both statable and both cheaper to fix than what they replace. First, presumed negatives: 1,942 sections are negative because no editorial note was found, and I showed today that one query phrase finds 184 sections while the union of six finds 306 - so single-phrase harvesting undercounts positives by ~40% and mislabels some negatives. Fix: harvest the union, and derive the label mechanically by diffing point-in-time section text bracketing the effective date, which also multiplies the positive pool and removes the presumed-negative problem entirely. Second, cost: an agent reading 55 sections per rule is expensive - which is exactly why triage is a design choice worth measuring rather than a nuisance.

=== BOTTOM LINE ===

Do not abandon. I could not name a better project and I tried; the alternatives are a dead Erratum Gate (0.675 vs 0.675, p = 1.00 across four configurations) and a from-scratch idea at hour 51 with a 1.4% survival prior and no time to kill-test it. But do not adopt the sequence/ledger reframe either: I measured its pool at 1.31% of items and 2 of 42 positives, its modal instance is correct drafting rather than defect, and its mechanism is a compiler. Reframe on SCALE instead. It is the same corpus, the same labels, the same freeze, strictly less construction work, a 2.12% base rate that forecloses every constant and every cheap script by arithmetic, and it converts three capabilities from claimed to necessary.
audits.what_a_27_of_30_looks_like:
A submission scoring 27+/30 on this row answers "which design choices helped the agent solve the problem?" with a causal chain that has a number on every link and a control on every claim. Concretely, six things, all of which the scale reframe makes cheap and the current framing makes expensive:

1. THE HEADLINE DELTA BELONGS TO THE CAPABILITIES, NOT TO THE CORPUS. Report B0 (instruction only), B0-agent (instruction + point-in-time text, general tools, no skill/memory), and A1, with B0-agent explicitly labelled "this is the baseline, not my result" - section 7.3 already says this and it must survive contact with the README. The 30-point claim is A1 minus B0-agent, and it must be positive with McNemar p < 0.05, clustered by FR document. Under the scale framing this is a paired comparison over ~2,000 section-decisions, not 84, so it is powerable.

2. A SCRIPT CONTROL PER CAPABILITY. For each capability, the same capability implemented as deterministic code, scored on the same cases. anchor_resolve as a tool the agent calls vs anchor_resolve run exhaustively by a script that flags any unresolved anchor. I measured that script today: 0.45-0.49 accuracy against a 0.5758 constant on the labelled subset, and at rule level the best cheap script tops out at F1 0.110 against a 0.0415 constant. Publishing "here is my own capability, weaponised against me, and it scores 0.11" is the single most convincing artefact available, and it is the direct answer to "why an agent at all?"

3. LEAVE-ONE-OUT ABLATIONS, THREE OF THEM, EACH x3 RUNS WITH VARIANCE. Not "we added three things and the number went up." A1, A1-minus-tool, A1-minus-skill, A1-minus-memory, on identical cases, with pass@3 and the spread. Any capability whose leave-one-out delta is inside the run-to-run spread gets demoted to the removed-experiment row and SAID SO - which is also the mandatory negative result, obtained honestly rather than staged.

4. THE TOOL-AVAILABILITY VS TOOL-USE GAP, MEASURED. Give the agent anchor_resolve with no skill file and count how often it calls it, and on how many of the section's instructions before ruling. In the pilot both clean-item errors were premature rulings on a partial read. If the agent has the tool and rules after checking instruction 1 of 7, that is a number - "called the tool on 2.1 of 5.4 instructions before ruling" - and SKILL.md moving it to 5.2 with an accuracy delta is the cleanest causal chain in the whole rubric. This is the specific thing that separates a purposeful capability from a bolted-on one, and almost nobody in the field will produce it.

5. PER-FAILURE-CLASS DELTAS, NOT AVERAGES. This is the project's own hot take (7.9) applied to itself: report false-defect rate and missed-defect rate per arm, and recall broken out by defect class (missing quoted anchor / unresolvable designation / hierarchy-level mismatch). I measured that the quoted-anchor class is ~21% of the labelled 2017+ pool and ~51% of the population - so an average will hide which class each capability actually moved. At a 2.12% base rate the false-alarm number IS the story.

6. THE HUMAN CHECKPOINT AT ONE NAMED FAILURE MODE, JUSTIFIED BY A MEASUREMENT. Not a blanket approval gate. "The agent abstains and routes to the drafter on exactly the class where its precision measured below X" - one gate, one number, one reason.

The shape a judge is looking for is: observed failure -> capability chosen to fix that failure -> ablation isolating it -> script control proving an agent was needed -> per-class delta showing what it cost. Five links, five numbers. Three capabilities with that treatment beats six capabilities without it, and the PDF says so outright.

The advanced solution has no measured evidence that ANY of its three capabilities helps. Every number in the project is a statement about the corpus, not about the agent design.

Unpacked: 0.500 -> 0.818 is the gain from giving the agent the section text, and the kill test itself classifies that arm as B0-agent, a sanctioned baseline type 2. The 30-point row scores what happens ON TOP of that, and there is not one measurement of it anywhere. And when I implemented capability 1 myself today it scored at chance (0.4545-0.4848 against a 0.5758 constant, n = 33), and capability 3's target class measured at 2 positive items in the entire labelled pool. Building the best benchmark in the field and the median agent inside it optimises the wrong 30 points.

rivals.angle:
STOP PREDICTING THE OUTCOME OF THE PROCEDURE. MAKE THE AGENT RUN THE PROCEDURE.

The incumbent asks a binary question ("will this instruction execute?"). Binary questions have a 0.500 constant floor by construction, which is why the incumbent must spend its whole design budget on exact instruction-count matching just to get back to chance, and why its headline gain is retrieval. Every rival below asks the agent to *execute the amendment and emit the resulting CFR text*. That single move changes three things at once: the constant floor drops from 0.500 to a MEASURED 0.000; state-carried-across-steps stops being an argument and becomes load-bearing by construction; and the agent's output stops being a label and becomes the artifact the user actually needs.

FOUR THINGS I MEASURED THIS SESSION THAT CHANGE THE DECISION:

(1) INFRASTRUCTURE — THE INCUMBENT'S CORPUS IS UNREACHABLE FROM THIS MACHINE. ecfr.gov returns HTTP 403 "Your IP address has been blocked - Support Code 02" on EVERY path (homepage, /api/versioner, /api/search), browser UA or not. federalregister.gov/api returned HTTP 200 at 06:49 UTC and the identical 74-byte block by 06:51, still 403 after a pause. The incumbent's §7.6 corpus (eCFR search + eCFR versioner + FR API) is 100% blocked. govinfo.gov is fully open and is a complete substitute: CFR annual editions 1996-2026, FR daily XML back to 1994, ECFR current bulk, plus api.govinfo.gov/search on DEMO_KEY. Every rival below is built on govinfo ONLY. This alone is worth escalating regardless of which task wins.

(2) THE HARVEST IS BETTER THAN THE INCUMBENT'S AND I RAN IT END TO END. The CFR annual edition's own <CITA> source credit carries dated FR citations verbatim — "[81 FR 62386, Sept. 9, 2016, as amended at 88 FR 67962, Oct. 3, 2023]". Diffing the CITA between edition Y and Y+1 yields, mechanically and with zero authored judgement, the exact ordered set of FR documents OFR applied in that window, each with the date that resolves to a govinfo FR daily XML file. VERIFIED on 8 issues, HTTP 200 each.

(3) THE INCUMBENT'S NAMED BUILD RISK IS SOLVED. Its §8 item 2 says the AMDPAR attributor is the weak link and ran at 0.46 completeness, with an H4 STOP gate at 0.90. On the largest rule in my sample (88 FR 36894 — 423 amendatory instructions across 67 sections), the rule "an AMDPAR names a section, else it inherits the previous one" attributes 422/423 = 99.8%. One bug remains: it does not reset at a <REGTEXT> part boundary.

(4) A CONTAMINATION SOURCE NOBODY HAS NAMED. The pre-edition contains <EFFDNOTP> "Effective Date Note" blocks that quote the pending amendment verbatim; § 52.2587's says, literally, "For the convenience of the user, the revised and added text is set forth as follows:". The input edition ships the answer. Must be stripped with <CITA>, <EDNOTE>, <EAR>. Also: annual editions carry a global typographic normalisation (U+2013 -> ASCII hyphen) that fakes 107 "changed" sections in title 40 vol 5 where only 24 changed and only 9 were amended.

VARIANTS I KILLED SO THE PARENT DOESN'T RE-DERIVE THEM. (a) "Write the amendment that codifies this change", scored by executing the emitted instruction — dies instantly: "Revise § X to read as follows: <entire after-text>" is a valid amendment that executes perfectly, and a diff-to-AMDPAR compiler beats any model on minimality too. (b) "Which other sections' cross-references break after a redesignation" — a grep over the CFR for the old designation is the correct answer. (c) "Which instruction did the agency later correct" (ground truth = FR "Final rule; correction" documents, ~250/yr, one of which reads "Amendatory instruction 2 in the interim rule contained a typographical error") — concrete and mechanically labelled, but I have NOT measured the positional prior on the corrected instruction index, and a 3-line "always guess instruction 2" attack could plausibly win. One hour would settle it; I did not spend it, so I am not proposing it.

THE ONE ARGUMENT THAT FAVOURS THE INCUMBENT AND I WILL NOT HIDE IT: the incumbent has a MEASURED agent arm (0.545 -> 0.818 on 11 clean items). None of my three rivals has one. I measured the floor, the pool, the harvest and the attacks; I did not run a model. The mirror-image risk is real: exact-match reconstruction may floor the agent out too. Every rival below therefore carries an explicit H5 abort gate — one deterministic applier plus one agent on 12 items; if the agent cannot clear 0.30 exact-match, abandon and fall back to the incumbent, which by then shares 80% of the same harvest code.

proposals.name: Codify — replay the amendment, don't predict it
proposals.task: One item = (CFR section, one annual-edition window). The agent is given the section text exactly as the printed CFR had it at edition Y (with <CITA>, <EDNOTE>, <EFFDNOTP>, <EAR> stripped), plus the ordered amendatory instructions from every Federal Register final rule that OFR applied to that section during the window, plus each rule's DATES block. It must emit the resulting section text — i.e. do the Office of the Federal Register's codification job. Gold is OFR's own printed text for edition Y+1. The user is the regulations drafter or OFR liaison of the incumbent's §7.1, but instead of handing her a WILL_FAIL/WILL_EXECUTE label she gets the codified section she can paste into her rule package and read.
proposals.why_agent_row_scores_high: Three capabilities, each load-bearing by construction rather than by argument, and each with an ablation whose result is forced. (1) TOOL — apply_edit(state, operation, anchor, designation) does the verbatim text surgery deterministically and REFUSES when the anchor is absent; the model does interpretation, the tool does execution. Ablation 'agent emits the full section text directly' is the cleanest possible demonstration that LLMs cannot reproduce 5-30KB verbatim, and it is a number, not an opinion. (2) MEMORY — the section-state ledger: instruction n executes against the text instructions 1..n-1 left behind. Ablation 'apply every instruction to the original pre-text' scores 0.000 by construction on the chained items — I have the receipts in §hard_case. (3) VERIFICATION — after the replay, check designation uniqueness and contiguity and hierarchy well-formedness, and re-resolve any anchor that missed at a looser normalisation level; report the catch rate. This directly answers the rubric's 'which design choices helped the agent solve the problem' with three forced answers instead of one soft one ('we gave it the document'). It also produces the deliverable micro1 actually buys: a per-instruction trajectory where every step names an anchor, a resolution level and a resulting state.
