proposals.primary_metric: Codification exact-match — the fraction of (section, window) items whose reconstructed text equals OFR's printed edition-Y+1 text after ONE published normalisation function (unicode dash/quote/space folding, whitespace collapse, and removal of <CITA>/<EDNOTE>/<EFFDNOTP>/<EAR>). Scorer is Python stdlib string equality: no model, no network, no dependencies, no hand-picked keys. Secondary diagnostics, all deterministic: edit-set precision and recall over difflib opcodes (so a near-miss is visible and the changelog can say which edits were lost); accuracy as a function of replay depth k; and — critically — the score reported SEPARATELY for the two strata I measured, the 'quoted-result' stratum where the answer text appears verbatim in the FR document and the 'assembled-result' stratum where it does not. Across 1,173 AMDPARs in 4 FR issues the assembled stratum is ~45% of all instructions (remove 27.2%, remove-X-add-Y-in-its-place 14.2%, redesignate 2.6%, remove-and-reserve 1.1%). The headline is the assembled stratum; the quoted stratum is reported beside it, never blended. Guard metric: a 'purity gate' — the fraction of items whose pre->post diff is confined to designations the AMDPARs actually name — printed before any headline number, the same way the incumbent gates on attributor completeness. DO NOT use character similarity as the metric; see the attack table for why.
proposals.trivial_attack_and_why_it_fails: I built and ran the attacks on the 9 clean title-40 items. NONE WINS, AND THE FLOOR IS 0.000, NOT 0.500. A1 identity (echo the pre-text unchanged): 0/9 exact, mean char-similarity 0.9318. A2 echo the FR document: 0/9, sim 0.0072. B copy-splice — append every 'to read as follows' tail found in the FR document, which is the obvious 15-liner: 0/9 exact, sim 0.4302. C, the strongest ~20-line no-model executor I could write — literal substitution for every `removing "X" and adding in its place "Y"`, plus paragraph deletion for `removing paragraph (x)`, plus the copy-splice: 0/9 exact, and mean sim 0.4303, i.e. IT IS WORSE THAN DOING NOTHING (0.9318). Naive text surgery destroys the section. No constant, no lookup, no regex and no majority class scores above zero, because there is nothing to be constant about — the answer is 5-30 KB of text, not a class label. TWO THINGS I MUST SAY AGAINST MYSELF. First, that 0.9318 identity similarity is the reason character-similarity metrics are BANNED here: doing nothing looks like 93% correct. Only exact-match and edit-set F1 have an honest floor, and the build must never quote a similarity number as a headline. Second and more serious: the honest strongest attack is NOT 20 lines. A competent 300-600 line deterministic AMDPAR interpreter — a real compiler for OFR's amendatory sublanguage — would score materially above zero, and I did not build one. My estimate is 0.30-0.60 exact-match on the assembled stratum and it is UNMEASURED. That interpreter is PDF baseline type 3 and the build must ship it as the baseline, loudly, at H5, before any agent number is published. The claim is not 'no script can do this'; the claim is 'the trivial script scores exactly zero and the serious script is the baseline'.
proposals.hard_case: The cross-rule state dependency, and I found three in a nine-item sample rather than arguing it exists. § 52.2540: rule 1 (88 FR 36895, 5 Jun 2023) says 'b. Adding paragraph (c).'; rule 2 (88 FR 67107, 29 Sep 2023) says 'b. Redesignating paragraph (c) as paragraph (c)(1) and adding paragraph (c)(2).' Rule 2 redesignates a paragraph that did not exist until rule 1 created it. Apply rule 2 to the original pre-text and the anchor is absent — the no-ledger ablation is not merely worse, it is 0.000 by construction. § 52.2356 is sharper still: rule 1 is '24. Add § 52.2356 to read as follows:' — the section does not exist at edition Y — and rule 2 then redesignates paragraph (b) as (b)(1) inside it. § 52.2283 is the third (rule 1 revises (d)(3) and adds (d)(4),(5),(e); rule 2 adds (d)(6) and redesignates (e) as (e)(1)). Measured chained-item rate: 3/9 in title-40 vol5 and 22/70 in title-42 vol5, so ~30% of the pool is hard, not a curated anecdote — which is exactly what the incumbent's own hard case failed to be (its splits: 13 genuine instances from 6 documents, 0 of which survive its own filter).
proposals.beats_incumbent_because: Six measured margins, not a preference. (1) FLOOR: 0.000 measured against four attacks versus the incumbent's 0.500 constant — the incumbent spends its entire eval design on exact instruction-count matching just to drag a constant back down to chance, and its best model-free feature (0.5934) only survives because its own permutation null says p=0.185. Here there is nothing to neutralise. (2) POOL: 70 clean items from ONE volume-year pair, 22 of them chained, versus the incumbent's 42 pairs (n=84) scraped from a whole-corpus search, of which its pilot could only use 11. (3) THE INCUMBENT'S OWN STOP GATE: its H4 rule is 'attributor completeness < 0.90 -> stop and fix before anything else', and its pilot ran at 0.46; I measured 422/423 = 99.8% on a 423-instruction rule using a five-line carry-forward rule. (4) CORPUS REACHABILITY: eCFR and the FR API both 403 this machine right now; this runs on govinfo, verified. (5) THE 30-POINT ROW: the incumbent's honest answer to 'which design choices helped' is 'we gave the agent the document' — a +27 pp retrieval gain on 11 items with McNemar p=0.375. Here the answer is three capabilities each with a forced ablation, one of which (the ledger) is provably 0.000 without it. (6) END-TO-END QUALITY (20 pts): the output is the codified section text a drafter can read and sign, not a two-valued label. And the incumbent is not lost — it becomes a stratum of this pool.
proposals.honest_weakness: NO AGENT ARM WAS RUN. I measured the floor, the pool, the harvest, the contamination and the attacks; I did not put a model on it. Exact-match reconstruction of a 5-30 KB section is genuinely hard and the agent may floor out alongside the scripts, which would be a symmetric failure and would leave the incumbent — which at least has 0.545 -> 0.818 on 11 items — as the safer bet. Pre-registered abort gate: at H5, run the deterministic applier plus one agent on 12 items; if agent exact-match < 0.30, abandon and fall back, by which point 80% of the harvest code is shared. Second: gold contamination by OFR's own typesetting. Some edition-to-edition differences are re-flow and re-lettering unrelated to any amendment, and my unicode normalisation removed the obvious layer (107 apparent changes -> 24) but I have NOT measured the residual; the purity gate must be computed and printed before any headline. Third: the serious 300-600 line interpreter baseline is unmeasured and could land at 0.5+, compressing the improvement — that is the number most likely to embarrass the submission and it must be produced early, not late. Fourth: my whole measurement is one volume of one title of one year pair (EPA state implementation plans, which skew toward table and add operations); the title-42 CMS generality check was item-count only, not attack-scored.

proposals.name: Codify or Refuse — execution with a restraint class
proposals.task: Codify, plus a minority class the agent must decline. Every item is a (section, window) replay as above, but the pool deliberately includes sections where OFR could NOT execute the instruction and published an editorial note saying so ('§ X was amended; however, a portion of the amendment could not be incorporated due to inaccurate amendatory instruction'). For each item the agent emits either the reconstructed section text, or CANNOT_EXECUTE naming the failing instruction and the anchor that did not resolve. It has to discover inexecutability by attempting the work, not guess it from surface features. The user is unchanged — the drafter clearing a rule — but she now gets, in one pass, either the codified text or the specific instruction that will not run and the reason.
proposals.why_agent_row_scores_high: Same three capabilities as Codify, but the verification capability stops being hygiene and becomes the decision. The anchor_resolve tool's refusal signal IS the answer for the negative class, so 'we added verification' is backed by a class-specific recall number rather than a vibe. It also lands squarely on two things micro1 publishes about its own benchmarks: restraint scored as a first-class outcome ('the benchmark rewards restraint as much as it rewards extraction', Realm Pathology) and per-class results never blended ('a system that quietly fails the hardest documents and posts a high score on the easy ones cannot hide behind a single blended number', LongExtractBench). Per-class recall on the refusal class versus the execution class is the natural headline, and it is exactly the shape of the incumbent's own hot take about per-class recall — except here it is the primary metric rather than a postscript.
proposals.corpus: Codify's corpus plus a refusal-class harvest, all from govinfo. api.govinfo.gov/search with DEMO_KEY, VERIFIED live: {"query":"collection:CFR \"could not be incorporated\""} returns count=86; "inaccurate amendatory instruction" returns count=52. Results are section-level granules (e.g. packageId CFR-2026-title15-vol2, granuleId CFR-2026-title15-vol2-sec742-6) with a direct per-section XML link, which is a clean harvest primitive and needs no eCFR. Those counts span multiple annual editions so distinct sections are fewer — call it 30-50 pending dedup, which I did not run. ENRICHMENT WORTH TAKING: Federal Register 'Final rule; correction' documents are far more numerous than NARA's editorial notes — I counted 2, 0, 4 and 1 correction-titled RULE documents in four FR issues (~250/yr), and one of them reads verbatim 'Amendatory instruction 2 in the interim rule contained a typographical error; this document corrects this typographical error.' That is an agency-authored defective-instruction label with a far larger pool than the 92 editorial notes the incumbent is built on.
proposals.licence: Identical to Codify — 17 U.S.C. §105, govinfo/GPO, bulkdata sitemapped rather than disallowed. The only addition is api.govinfo.gov, which needs DEMO_KEY or a free key; that is harvest-time only and the frozen artifact the judge runs is offline.
proposals.primary_metric: A single penalised-guessing score over the combined pool, published alongside its two components and never in place of them: +1 for an exactly-correct reconstruction on an executable item, +1 for CANNOT_EXECUTE on an item OFR flagged, 0 for silence, and a stated negative for confidently emitting text on a section OFR could not codify. Both class recalls printed separately, plus the reconciliation line success + failure == n_cases that micro1's own grader prints. Scorer: string equality against a NARA-authored fact plus string equality against OFR's printed text. No model, no network.
proposals.trivial_attack_and_why_it_fails: This is the strongest foreclosure of the three and it is structural. THERE IS NO CONSTANT POLICY THAT SCORES ABOVE ZERO. Always-CANNOT_EXECUTE earns nothing on the execution class, because that class demands the actual text — it does not collect the 0.500 that the incumbent's binary framing hands it for free. Always-attempt earns nothing on the refusal class and, per Codify's measured attack table, 0/9 on the execution class too (identity 0/9, copy-splice 0/9, 20-line executor 0/9 and worse than identity by similarity). The incumbent's entire eval-design budget goes to exact instruction-count matching so that a constant cannot beat 0.500; here the constant collects zero because guessing the label is not the task. The residual attack surface is a feature threshold on the refusal class alone — the incumbent measured its best such feature at 0.5934 with an empirical p=0.185 against its own permutation null — but that attack can only ever address the minority class, and it earns nothing on the majority class where the answer is text. HONEST CAVEAT, SAME AS CODIFY: the serious 300-600 line AMDPAR interpreter is the real baseline and is unmeasured; it would additionally get the refusal class partly for free, since 'my interpreter threw' is a plausible CANNOT_EXECUTE signal. That interpreter must be built and reported, and if it clears ~0.6 combined this proposal is weaker than it looks.
proposals.hard_case: The instruction that is individually valid and collectively defective — the incumbent's own §7.7 hard case, but here it is DISCOVERED by execution rather than predicted. A rule whose instruction 12 removes a paragraph that instruction 5 already redesignated: every instruction resolves in isolation, so a per-instruction checker passes them all, and only the ledger sees the collision. My § 52.2540 and § 52.2356 pairs are the benign version of exactly this shape (rule 2 operating on paragraphs rule 1 created), which is direct evidence the defective version exists in the same population. Route unresolved collisions to a single named human checkpoint with both readings and the paragraph trace — one checkpoint at one named failure mode, which is what micro1's own Chief Economist argues for and the opposite of a blanket approval gate.
proposals.beats_incumbent_because: It contains the incumbent as a strictly weaker special case. The incumbent asks the drafter to accept a two-valued guess whose constant floor is 0.500 and whose measured agent gap (0.545 -> 0.818) is Fisher p=0.36 at n=11 and by its own admission 'not statistically established'. This asks the agent to do the work, and inexecutability falls out of the attempt with the failing anchor attached — which is the answer the drafter can act on, because 'this will fail' without naming the instruction is not actionable. Every Codify margin applies (0.000 floor measured, 99.8% attributor, govinfo reachable while eCFR 403s, pool 70/volume), and on top of them the constant-policy foreclosure is complete rather than engineered: the incumbent has to design its pool to neutralise a constant, this one has nothing for a constant to grip.
proposals.honest_weakness: Pool depth on the refusal class is the real risk and I did not resolve it. 86 and 52 granule hits are across multiple annual editions, so distinct sections could be 30-50 or could be 20; each also needs its pre-text and its defective rule resolved, which will cut further. If it lands under ~15 the class is too thin to carry a per-class recall number and the design collapses back to Codify. The FR-correction enrichment (~250/yr) is the mitigation but I only inspected three correction documents and did not build a parser for their loci, so its usable yield is UNMEASURED. Second risk: a combined penalised score is easy to accuse of being tuned — the penalty weight is authored by me, which is exactly the self-serving-rubric trap the PDF warns about; the mitigation is to publish the raw per-class counts and let the weight be a footnote, never the headline. Third: this is the most work of the three — Codify plus a second harvest plus a second metric — and it is the one most likely to be 80% finished at the deadline. Fourth, same as Codify: no agent arm was run, and here the agent must be good at two different things.

proposals.name: The Part Ledger — codification at a scale one context cannot hold
proposals.task: Move the unit from one section to one whole CFR part for one annual-edition window. The agent receives the part as printed at edition Y (routinely 0.5-3 MB) plus every final rule that touched any of its sections during the window (measured: 20 distinct FR issues for title-42 vol5 alone), and must emit the part as OFR printed it at edition Y+1. It has to decide which rules touch which sections, in what order, and carry a shared ledger across all of them, because rules interleave across sections and one rule's redesignation changes the anchors another rule depends on.
proposals.why_agent_row_scores_high: This is the only one of the three where ORCHESTRATION is honest rather than decorative. The input genuinely does not fit one context — that is a property of the corpus, not a contrived split — so a map-reduce over sections with a shared part-level ledger and a reduce-time conflict check is the design the problem forces, and the PDF's changelog example order (skill -> verification -> orchestration -> combine) is followed for a reason instead of for show. It is also the only variant where 'purposeful choices matter more than the number of components' can be demonstrated in the negative: run the same agent WITHOUT orchestration on the same part and watch it truncate, which is a measured failure a judge can see in one screenshot of the trajectory.
proposals.corpus: Identical govinfo sources; the difference is the unit and therefore the freeze size. Measured: title-42 vol5 2023->2024 needs 20 FR daily XML files (2.0-6.3 MB each, ~80 MB) plus two CFR volumes (~12 MB) to cover 70 amended sections in 1,180. So a two-part freeze is ~100 MB with a SHA-256 manifest, offline, network-off — comfortable. What is NOT comfortable is the per-run token cost, which is the reason for the rating below.
proposals.licence: Identical to Codify — 17 U.S.C. §105, govinfo/GPO bulkdata, sitemapped not disallowed, no key.
proposals.primary_metric: Per-section codification exact-match across every amended section in the part (so a part with 70 amended sections contributes 70 scored units and the ≥10-case floor is cleared by a single part), reported alongside a part-level all-correct rate — the metric OFR's own job is actually graded on, and one that will be well under 1.0 and therefore non-saturating. Secondary: sections spuriously modified (the agent must not touch the ~1,110 sections the rules do not name — a false-edit rate, which is the restraint metric and the natural degenerate-lane closer), and accuracy versus replay depth k. Scorer: stdlib string equality per section, no model.
proposals.trivial_attack_and_why_it_fails: Every Codify attack applies unchanged and each was measured at 0/9 exact — identity 0.000, echo-the-FR-document 0.000, copy-splice 0.000, the 20-line executor 0.000 and worse than identity by similarity. The part-level unit adds one attack of its own that a script CAN partly win and I want it on the record: 'copy the whole edition-Y part through unchanged' scores 0 on every amended section but is trivially right on the ~1,110 untouched ones — which is precisely why the metric is defined over amended sections only, and why the false-edit rate is reported beside it rather than folded in. Anyone who quotes a part-level number that includes untouched sections is reporting ~94% for doing nothing, and the README must say so before a judge says it. Same honest caveat as the other two: the serious 300-600 line interpreter is unmeasured, and at part level it would additionally get section routing for free from the <REGTEXT PART=> attribute.
proposals.hard_case: Two rules amending the same section with interleaved effective dates, inside a part where a third rule redesignates paragraphs that the first two anchor on. § 52.2540 is the two-rule core of this in my measured sample (88 FR 36895 adds paragraph (c); 88 FR 67107 then redesignates (c) as (c)(1)); at part level that same collision has to be detected while 69 other sections are in flight and no single instruction is individually wrong. The no-ledger ablation is 0.000 by construction, and unlike the section-level version the failure is also visible as a cross-section inconsistency, which is what the human checkpoint is for.
proposals.beats_incumbent_because: It is the only formulation on this corpus where the orchestration capability is forced by the input rather than chosen by the contestant, which is the single most defensible answer to 'which design choices helped the agent solve the problem' — and orchestration is the capability the incumbent's three-capability design does not use at all. It inherits every Codify margin (0.000 measured floor versus a 0.500 constant, 99.8% attributor versus the incumbent's 0.46 and its own 0.90 stop gate, govinfo reachable while the incumbent's eCFR and FR API both 403 this machine) and adds a per-section metric that clears the ≥10-case floor from a single part with 70 units, against the incumbent's 11 usable pilot items. It also produces by far the strongest video: one part, twenty rules, one ledger, and a collision the agent catches at reduce time.
proposals.honest_weakness: I rate this probably_not in 24 hours solo and I would not start here. Per-run cost and wall-clock are the killers: three arms times three runs over a 1-3 MB part with 20 rules is a lot of tokens and a lot of minutes, and the PDF requires cost-per-task and human-time-per-task reported from run one, so a design whose cost row is embarrassing is self-defeating. It also front-loads all of Codify's unmeasured risks (no agent arm, unmeasured gold-typesetting purity, unmeasured serious-interpreter baseline) behind a much slower feedback loop, which is the worst possible combination when the abort gate needs to fire at H5. The correct use of this proposal is as Codify's stretch tier: build Codify, and if the H5 gate passes comfortably, promote one part to a part-level case as the single hard case and the video centrepiece — which gets most of the orchestration credit for a fraction of the risk.

rivals.angle:
ARCHITECTURE FIRST, THEN THE VERDICT ON YOUR REFRAME, THEN TWO FINDINGS THAT CHANGE THE BUILD PLAN REGARDLESS OF WHICH PROJECT YOU PICK.

**The architecture that scores 27+/30.** The 30-point row asks one question: "Which design choices helped the agent solve the problem?" The strongest possible answer is not a big delta from three capabilities stacked together. It is a **diagonal ablation matrix**: an evaluation set partitioned into disjoint case classes, where removing capability K collapses class K and leaves the others untouched. That converts "which design choices helped" from an essay into a table. Almost nobody in a 500-entry field will produce one, because it requires designing the *eval set* around the *architecture* rather than the reverse. The incumbent cannot produce one: it has one number (0.545 -> 0.818) driven by one capability (context), and its own §7.4 already concedes capability 3 may have to be demoted to the removed experiment. That is a 22-24/30 answer, not 27+.

**Verdict on the sequence reframe: it works, but not as stated, and it forces a metric change.** I measured it. In one month of Federal Register rules (March 2024, n=249 rules / 1,812 amendatory instructions): 15.7% of rules have a section receiving >=2 instructions, 4.8% have a redesignation inside such a section, and **6.4% of rules (2.65% of instructions) carry an explicit "newly redesignated" reference** — an instruction whose anchor does not exist in the before-text and is created by an earlier instruction in the same rule. Live example, verified: `§ 98.16 ... b. Redesignating paragraphs (x) through (ii) as (bb) through (ll); c. Adding new paragraphs (x) through (aa); d. Revising newly redesignated paragraphs (ee) and (ff).` Paragraph (ee) is nowhere in the before-text. So sequence is real and it is countable. But two corrections to the reframe as you posed it. (1) The interesting class is not "collectively defective rules" — those are rare and unlabelled. It is the mirror image: **legitimate rules on which every state-blind system fires a false defect, by construction, 100% of the time.** That is a structural guarantee, not a hope that the LLM does better. (2) It cannot carry the headline under a binary WILL_FAIL/WILL_EXECUTE metric with a 0.500 chance floor and n=84 — the class is 6.4% of rules, so it moves the headline by ~3 points and vanishes in the noise the incumbent already admits to (Fisher p=0.36). **To make sequence the centrepiece you must move the metric from binary classification to instruction-level localisation.** Then chance drops from 0.500 to ~1/k (median k=7 instructions per rule), the permutation-null apparatus becomes unnecessary, and the state-dependent class becomes a scored precision term rather than a rounding error. All three proposals below do this.

**Finding 1, and it is urgent: the incumbent's corpus is currently unreachable from your build machine.** `ecfr.gov`, `federalregister.gov` and `ecfr.federalregister.gov` all return **HTTP 403** with the body `"Your IP address has been blocked - please contact support / Support Code 02"` — robots.txt, /api/search, /api/versioner and /api/v1/documents.json alike, browser UA no help. This is not a general outage: govinfo.gov, api.github.com, clinicaltrials.gov and api.fda.gov all returned 200 in the same minute. Most likely cause is yesterday's kill-test harvest. The incumbent's plan puts that harvest on hours H1-H4 of the critical path and calls it "the risk"; right now it is a wall.

**Finding 2: govinfo replaces both APIs and de-risks the incumbent's three worst problems.** `www.govinfo.gov/bulkdata` is 200 and needs no key. It carries ECFR, CFR annual editions **back to 1996**, and FR daily/monthly XML at 12-13 MB/month (~1.3 GB for 2017-2026, freezable). Three consequences, each measured: (a) the FR XML wraps each `<AMDPAR>` and the `<SECTION>` it targets inside the same `<REGTEXT TITLE PART>` element — **AMDPAR-to-section attribution is a structural parse, not a heuristic**, so the incumbent's 0.46 attributor completeness (its stated highest-value build task) is an artifact of the source it chose, not a hard problem; (b) CFR annual editions from 1996 **remove the eCFR-2017 floor that cost the incumbent half its pool**; (c) defect labels are a structural element too — `<EDNOTE>` inside `<DIV8 TYPE="SECTION" N="§ 9.3">`.

**Finding 3, the one that fixes the incumbent's own "matters most" gap.** Its §8.1 says the 27-point gap is unestablished at n=24 and the whole build hinges on reaching n=84. There is a second, independent, agency-authored label channel it never looked at: **Federal Register correction documents**. 25-29 of 249 rules in March 2024 (10-11.6%) are corrections, and **3 of 249 (1.2%) name the defective amendatory instruction by its number** — verbatim: *"2. On page 1432, in the third column, in amendatory instruction 9, in § 170.315 correct paragraph (g)(3) by ..."*. That is ~36/year, ~320 over 2017-2026, on top of the ~90-150 OFR editorial notes — and it comes with an instruction-level localisation label rather than a section-level binary. Pool goes from 42 pairs to several hundred items, and the label gets richer at the same time.

**Finding 4, on the trivial attack, measured rather than argued.** I ran the strongest naive attack on real data: 57 quoted-anchor removal instructions from CFR title 31 in March 2024, checked against the CFR 2023 annual edition at three normalisation levels. Exact 73.7%, whitespace-only 1.8%, **not found at any level 12.3%, section absent from the edition 12.3%** — a **24.6% false-defect rate on instructions that overwhelmingly codified fine**. And the misses are diagnostic: `"§ 546.201(a)"` (an anchor the same rule creates) and `", but are not limited to,"` (a stale base). So the 20-line anchor check does not win; it has a precision problem that is exactly the two things the ledger and the exact-vintage base fix.

**What this means for the ranking.** Proposals 1 and 2 deliberately share the corpus with the incumbent. That is the right engineering call at 24 hours with a blocked API — the harvest is the risk, and govinfo collapses it — and it is consistent with "architecture leads, domain follows". They are rivals on architecture and metric, not on domain. Proposal 3 is the honest third: a distinct capability thesis, and I name the ten-line attack that beats it unless one field is stripped.

proposals.name: LEDGER — instruction-level codification defect localisation
proposals.task: Input: one Federal Register final rule's ordered amendatory instruction set for one CFR section, plus the codified section text as it stood immediately before the rule. Output: for each instruction, in order, a verdict EXECUTES or FAILS(designation, failure_class), plus the section state after execution. The agent is playing the Office of the Federal Register's codification desk. It is NOT a binary rule-level classifier — it must name which instruction fails and where.
proposals.why_agent_row_scores_high: This is the only design in the set that yields a genuinely diagonal ablation matrix, and each cell is pre-registerable before the run. THREE capabilities, three disjoint case classes, three predicted collapses. (1) TOOL — anchor_resolve(section_tree, quoted_text, designation, as_of): deterministic; reports presence of the quoted anchor at three normalisation levels (exact / whitespace-collapsed / alphanumeric) and whether the designation resolves in the (a)(1)(i)(A) hierarchy. Owns class D-quote (defects where a quoted phrase is absent). Predicted: remove it and D-quote recall goes to roughly the LLM's unaided string-matching rate. (2) MEMORY — the rule-level ledger, carrying designation->state across instructions so instruction k is evaluated against the text instructions 1..k-1 left. Owns class S (legitimate state-dependent instructions). Predicted: remove it and precision on S goes to ~0 by construction, because 'revise newly redesignated paragraph (ee)' has no (ee) in the before-text. This is a structural guarantee, not an empirical hope — it is the strongest single sentence available for the 30-point row. (3) VERIFICATION — post-conditions on the resulting tree: designation uniqueness, no orphaned children, no gap in the letter sequence, and a restraint rule that forbids ruling FAIL until every instruction has been read. Owns the false-defect rate on class C. Each capability is attached to a failure I can already point at in the data, and the removed-experiment slot is pre-committed: hand the agent the CURRENT eCFR text instead of the point-in-time text and show accuracy rising for the wrong reason (the current text leaks the label — after a failed amendment it still lacks the change).
proposals.corpus: All govinfo bulkdata, all fetched and parsed this session while ecfr.gov and federalregister.gov return 403. (a) DEFECT LABELS, channel 1: https://www.govinfo.gov/bulkdata/ECFR/title-{n}/ECFR-title{n}.xml — <EDNOTE> elements nested in <DIV8 N="§ 9.3" TYPE="SECTION">. Measured across titles 24/42/45 (12.5 + 22.9 + 14.2 MB): 106 EDNOTEs, of which 9 are codification defects (8 'could not be incorporated', 1 'does not exist'), 38 nomenclature, 9 effective-date. Extrapolates to ~90-150 nationally, consistent with the incumbent's eCFR count of 92. (b) DEFECT LABELS, channel 2 — NEW: https://www.govinfo.gov/bulkdata/FR/{yyyy}/{mm}/FR-{yyyy}-{mm}.zip, 12-13 MB/month. Correction documents are 25-29 of 249 rules in March 2024; 3 of 249 name the defective amendatory instruction by number. ~36/yr, ~320 for 2017-2026. (c) INSTRUCTIONS: the same FR XML. <REGTEXT TITLE="40" PART="55"> wraps <AMDPAR> together with the <SECTION> it targets — structural attribution. March 2024: 249 rules, 1,031 REGTEXT blocks, 1,812 AMDPARs; 52 rules with >=5 instructions, 34 with >=10, 23 with >=20. (d) BEFORE-TEXT: https://www.govinfo.gov/bulkdata/CFR/{yyyy}/title-{n}/CFR-{yyyy}-title{n}-vol{v}.xml, annual editions 1996-2026 (I downloaded 2023 and 2024). Frozen artifact: FR REGTEXT blocks for the selected rules + the matching annual-edition sections + a SHA-256 manifest. Judge runs network-off.
proposals.licence: CLEAN, and the cleanest of anything in the prior 143-candidate search. All three collections are US Government works produced by GPO/OFR/NARA, uncopyrightable under 17 U.S.C. §105. https://www.govinfo.gov/robots.txt returns 200 and does not disallow /bulkdata. No API key: api.govinfo.gov returns 401 without one, bulkdata does not (all my fetches were keyless). No SPDX tag is published by GPO, so the claim rests on §105 plus GPO's own no-copyright statement — say that in the README rather than asserting an SPDX id. The incorporation-by-reference copyright problem (ASTM/NFPA) does not touch the text: eCFR states it does not contain standards incorporated by reference. This is the only candidate in the whole search with no licence caveat at all.
proposals.primary_metric: Instruction-level defect-localisation F1, macro-averaged over rules, deterministic, stdlib only, no model anywhere in the scoring path. For each rule the agent emits a set of (instruction_index, designation) pairs it calls defective; gold is the same set derived mechanically from the EDNOTE text or the correction document's own 'in amendatory instruction N ... paragraph (g)(3)' phrasing. Reported next to it, never blended: false-defect rate on class C (clean, single-instruction) and on class S (clean, state-dependent) separately; per-failure-class recall using OFR's own vocabulary (paragraph-does-not-exist / phrase-does-not-appear / incorrect-designation / incomplete-text / portion-only); N_completed with a success+failure==n reconciliation line; tokens, wall-clock and cost per task per arm. Pre-registered 'good': macro-F1 >= 0.70 with false-defect rate <= 0.15 on C and <= 0.20 on S, and >= +0.12 F1 over the strongest script baseline with a paired bootstrap clustered by FR document.
proposals.trivial_attack_and_why_it_fails: THE STRONGEST 20-LINE ATTACK: parse each AMDPAR for a quoted anchor and a paragraph designation; test both against the before-text; emit FAIL for any instruction whose anchor or designation is absent. I RAN IT on real data — 57 quoted-anchor removal instructions, CFR title 31, FR March 2024, against the CFR 2023 annual edition, on instructions that overwhelmingly codified without incident. Result: exact match 73.7%, whitespace-normalised only 1.8%, NOT FOUND at any normalisation level 12.3%, section absent from the edition entirely 12.3%. **False-defect rate 24.6%.** It does not win. And the two misses are the two things the architecture exists to fix: '§ 546.201(a)' is an anchor the same rule creates, and ', but are not limited to,' is a stale-base artifact. On class S the attack is provably worse than that — 'revising newly redesignated paragraph (ee)' has no (ee) in the before-text, so precision on S is 0 by construction, for every state-blind system, always. THE HONEST PART: the script that would actually threaten this is not 20 lines. It is a ~250-line partial reimplementation of the OFR ledger — parse the designation hierarchy, execute redesignations, then check anchors against the updated tree. That script is the thesis of the project written in Python, and it MUST be built and reported as the type-3 baseline at hour H5. If it clears the agent, the project dies there. I have not measured it and I am not going to pretend the 24.6% settles it. The constant baselines are settled: always-EXECUTE scores F1 = 0 (it names no instruction); always-flag-everything scores recall 1.0 at precision ~1/7 (median instructions per rule), F1 ~ 0.25.
proposals.hard_case: Verified live in the March 2024 corpus, not invented: **42 CFR § 546.202** receives NINE instructions in one rule, including 'e. Redesignating paragraph (e) as paragraph (f).' followed by 'f. Redesignating Note to paragraph (d) of § 546.202 as paragraph (e).' Executed in order these are valid; executed in either isolation or reverse order, instruction f writes onto a designation that instruction e was supposed to have vacated. Second hard case, same class: **40 CFR § 98.16** — 'b. Redesignating paragraphs (x) through (ii) as paragraphs (bb) through (ll); c. Adding new paragraphs (x) through (aa); and d. Revising newly redesignated paragraphs (ee) and (ff).' Both are the pure form of your reframe, and both make a 60-second video: point at (ee), point at the before-text, show it is not there, show that the rule is nonetheless perfectly valid, and say that this is the case every state-blind checker gets wrong.
proposals.beats_incumbent_because: Five things, four of them measured. (1) The incumbent's chance floor is 0.500 on a binary; this one's is F1 ~0.25 for the degenerate flag-everything policy and 0 for the constant, so it needs no exact-instruction-count matching, no 26-feature permutation null, and no p=0.185 caveat in the README. (2) Its pool is ~90-150 (its own count: 92); this one adds the correction-document channel for ~320 more items with a RICHER label, which directly answers its §8.1 'MATTERS MOST' admission that the 27-point gap is unestablished at n=24. (3) Its stated highest-value build task is fixing the AMDPAR attributor, currently at 0.46 completeness; govinfo's <REGTEXT> makes attribution structural, so that task largely disappears. (4) Its stated hard pool constraint is that eCFR point-in-time starts at 2017, which cost it half its items; CFR annual editions run to 1996. (5) Its architecture story is 'we gave the agent the document', a +32-point retrieval gain with one capability doing all the work and capability 3 pre-flagged for possible removal; this one has three capabilities each owning a case class with a pre-registered collapse, one of which is guaranteed by construction rather than hoped for. And, decisively today: **its two data sources are returning HTTP 403 to this machine and this one's are 200.**
proposals.honest_weakness: Four. (1) The ~250-line ledger-aware script is unmeasured and it is the real adversary. If a careful deterministic reimplementation of the OFR procedure scores within 5 points of the agent, the honest conclusion is that this is a parsing problem with an LLM bolted on, and the project should be killed at H5 rather than shipped. (2) Class S is only 6.4% of rules in the wild, so the eval set must OVERSAMPLE it to make the ledger's contribution visible — that is a stratified, not a natural, sample and the README must say so in the same paragraph as the headline number. (3) The negative class is 'no defect recorded by OFR or the agency', not 'provably clean'; some defective rules were simply never noticed. Label noise is one-sided and un-eliminable, exactly like SEC comment letters, and it caps the false-defect metric's meaning. (4) Getting the EXACT-vintage before-text is harder than it looks — the annual edition is up to 12 months stale relative to a rule's date, which is precisely why 12.3% of my 57 anchors were not found. eCFR's point-in-time versioner solves this in one call and is currently 403; without it you must replay intervening rules to reconstruct the base, which is Proposal 2's engine. Budget for that, or restrict the pool to sections with no intervening amendment (measurable, and it shrinks the pool).

proposals.name: REPLAY — the codification chain
proposals.task: Given a CFR section's official text at annual edition year 0, and the ordered amendatory instructions from every Federal Register rule that touched it in years 1..N, produce the section's text at each annual checkpoint. The agent works step by step; step k's input is its OWN output from step k-1, never the original. Gold at each checkpoint is GPO's annual CFR edition for that year. The user-facing artifact is a codification worksheet: 'here is what your rule will actually do to the text, paragraph by paragraph' — the thing a Federal Register drafter cannot get today without the OFR desk doing it by hand.
proposals.why_agent_row_scores_high: MEMORY is the thesis, not a bolt-on, and the metric makes that provable rather than arguable. This is the technique from the PDF's Appendix Example 3 — 'each sentence can be correct while the series as a whole no longer feels coherent' — ported out of audio and into text, and the strategy brief measured that lane at 1 of 64 visible competitors because the whole field read 'podcast' as an ASR infrastructure problem. Three capabilities: (1) MEMORY — the carried paragraph tree. The scoring shape makes its contribution unmistakable: a system without it CANNOT produce step k, so its curve is not lower, it is undefined past step 1. (2) TOOL — a deterministic tree editor exposing exactly the OFR operation set (revise / add / remove / redesignate / remove-and-add-in-place / insert-in-alphabetical-order), so the model chooses the operation and the tool performs it exactly. This is model-plans/engine-executes, the pattern that guarantees the agent structurally cannot corrupt whitespace or lose a sibling paragraph — the same guardrail architecture already shipped in Nistula Assistance, so the design rationale is authentic rather than borrowed. (3) VERIFICATION — after each step, tree invariants plus a STARS-elision reconciliation check (the FR prints only the changed paragraph, with '* * *' standing for unchanged material, so every splice must be proved non-destructive). The changelog writes itself: each iteration's evidence is a shift in the divergence curve, which is a far more interesting artifact than a delta on one number.
proposals.corpus: Same two govinfo collections, both verified 200 this session. CHECKPOINTS: https://www.govinfo.gov/bulkdata/CFR/{yyyy}/title-{n}/CFR-{yyyy}-title{n}-vol{v}.xml, annual editions 1996-2026. I downloaded title 11 for 2023 and 2024 (2.82 MB / 2.81 MB, 584 sections each) and diffed them: 51 sections changed, 0 added, 0 removed — so one small volume yields 51 candidate chains for a single year-step, and there are 50 titles and 30 years. Each changed section carries its own <CITA> source credit naming the amending rules, e.g. '[71 FR 18612, Apr. 12, 2006, as amended at 87 FR 77478, Dec. 19, 2022]', which is how you find the instruction stream without a search API. INSTRUCTIONS: https://www.govinfo.gov/bulkdata/FR/{yyyy}/{mm}/FR-{yyyy}-{mm}.zip, indexed by the TITLE and PART attributes on <REGTEXT>. Item selection: parts with 4-8 amendment years in the window and modest instruction volume per year, so chains are long enough to compound and short enough to finish. Frozen artifact ships year-0 text + the instruction blocks; years 1..N are held out as labels and are NOT in the judge's clone.
proposals.licence: Identical to Proposal 1 and equally clean: GPO/OFR/NARA, 17 U.S.C. §105, govinfo robots.txt 200, /bulkdata not disallowed, no key needed. One extra note worth writing into the README: because the held-out labels are simply later annual editions, the freeze boundary is trivially auditable by a judge — they can see that the answer document is not in the clone, which is the property the prior 143-candidate search concluded was the ONLY structural escape from the retrieval law.
proposals.primary_metric: Steps-survived-before-first-divergence, mean over chains, with a step counted as survived only if the emitted section text matches the annual edition after a published whitespace/entity normalisation. Deterministic, stdlib difflib, no model. **This metric has no chance floor at all** — there is no coin to flip, the output space is the section text, so no permutation null, no exact-count matching, no p-value theatre. Secondary, reported alongside and never blended: per-step edit-set F1 (gold diff vs predicted diff over changed paragraphs) so partial credit exists and the metric does not degenerate to 'everybody dies at step 1'; per-operation-class accuracy using the measured operation mix (revise-to-read-as-follows 18.6%, remove 16.1%, remove-and-add-in-place 9.1%, add 8.0%, redesignate 4.7%, table 3.3%, alphabetical-insert 2.0%, definition-of 1.2%, nth-sentence 1.0%, wherever-it-appears 0.7%); tokens and cost per step. Pre-registered 'good': mean steps survived >= 60% of chain length, and the drop from step 1 to step N smaller than the script baseline's by a factor of 2.
proposals.trivial_attack_and_why_it_fails: Three attacks, ascending. (A) IDENTITY — emit year-0 text at every checkpoint. Scores exactly 0 on steps-survived past the first amendment and 0 on edit-set F1 (empty predicted diff, recall 0). Pinned. Note that a naive character-similarity metric would have scored identity ~0.98 — this is why the metric is exact-match-with-normalisation and not similarity, and it is worth saying so out loud. (B) THE STARS-SPLICER, ~60 lines — for each 'revise paragraph X to read as follows', take the <SECTION> block the FR prints after the AMDPAR and splice it in, using the '* * *' elisions to decide what to keep. This is the real adversary. From the measured operation mix it can attempt at most ~27% of instructions (revise 18.6% + add 8.0%) and it cannot attempt redesignation, removal, alphabetical insertion or nth-sentence targeting at all. Its failures compound: one botched step poisons every later step in the chain, so its divergence curve should fall off a cliff. (C) THE FULL TEMPLATED EXECUTOR, ~350 lines — a genuine partial reimplementation of the OFR procedure. **I have NOT measured B or C and that is this proposal's largest unknown.** They must be built and reported as the type-3 baseline in the first six hours, before the agent exists. My honest prior, from the operation mix and from the 24.6% naive-anchor false-defect rate I did measure in Proposal 1, is that (B) survives 1-2 steps and (C) survives 3-4 on a 6-step chain — but a prior is not a measurement and I will not dress it as one. If (C) matches the agent's curve, kill it.
proposals.hard_case: A chain in which year 3 redesignates a block of paragraphs and year 5 amends one of the redesignated ones by its NEW letter. Getting year 5 right is impossible unless year 3 was right — this is the memory trap in its purest form and it is exactly the PDF's 'include one case that depends on a recurring detail'. The March 2024 corpus already shows the single-rule version (§ 178.601: 'Redesignate paragraphs (g)(6) through (8) as (g)(7) through (9); Add new paragraph (g)(6); Revise newly redesignated paragraph (g)(8)'); the multi-year version is the same mechanism with a two-year gap, and it makes the failure visible on screen — the memoryless arm edits a paragraph that has not existed for two years.
proposals.beats_incumbent_because: It removes every statistical apparatus the incumbent needs to defend itself. The incumbent's metric is a binary at a 0.500 chance floor, which forced it into exact instruction-count matching, a 26-feature permutation null, and an honest admission that its own best model-free feature sits inside that null at p=0.185 — and it still cannot establish its headline (Fisher p=0.36, McNemar p=0.375, n=11 clean items). REPLAY's metric has no chance line to defend against, so none of that machinery is needed. It also inverts the incumbent's central weakness on the 30-point row: where the incumbent's gain comes from handing the agent a document (retrieval, one capability, one number, and a capability-3 that its own plan says may have to be deleted), REPLAY's gain comes from a metric that a memoryless system cannot even attempt — which is the single most direct answer available to 'which design choices helped the agent solve the problem?'. And it occupies the one appendix technique the field left empty (1 of 64 visible entries), rather than the crowded verification-wrapper pattern the strategy brief flags as the field's median move.
proposals.honest_weakness: Three, and the first is serious. (1) I have NOT measured the templated-executor baseline, and this task is mechanical by design — OFR wrote the amendatory grammar to be executable. The 'closed-form anti-signal' law from the prior search (if you can check it in 20 lines you can often solve it in 200) points directly at this proposal. It is the highest-variance of the three and the one most likely to die in its own first six hours. (2) Difficulty calibration is a real risk in both directions: if chains are too hard everything dies at step 1 and the metric carries no signal; if too easy the agent saturates. The mitigation (per-step edit F1 plus careful part selection) is untested, and I would build a 2-step pilot before committing to 6-step chains. (3) Problem-and-user-value is thinner than Proposal 1's. 'Predict whether your rule will fail to codify' has a named user with a public exposure — 92 live editorial notes saying an agency's rule did not take effect as written. 'Reproduce the codified text' is a drafting-desk convenience, and the 15-point row will read weaker unless the artifact (the codification worksheet showing a drafter what her rule actually does to the text) carries it. Do not pitch this one on the benchmark; pitch it on the worksheet.

proposals.name: STALE BASE — defective instruction, or stale copy?
proposals.task: Three-way, per instruction: EXECUTES / DEFECTIVE(designation) / STALE_BASE(the missing authority). A drafter writes an amendatory instruction against her working copy of the CFR. When the anchor does not resolve, there are two completely different causes with identical symptoms: the instruction is wrong, or her copy is out of date because an intervening rule changed the section. Telling them apart is the drafter's actual daily failure mode, and the only way to do it is to reconstruct the exact-vintage base by replaying the intervening rules. The agent must also NAME the intervening authority it believes is missing, or abstain.
proposals.why_agent_row_scores_high: VERIFICATION-AS-RESTRAINT is the thesis, and it is the capability lane the strategy brief measured at 0 of 64 competitors while micro1's own published benchmark methodology says the opposite of what most entrants build: 'the benchmark rewards restraint as much as it rewards extraction ... the failures are less about getting facts wrong and more about saying more than the report allows.' Two capabilities only — the PDF's anti-kitchen-sink clause is satisfied by construction and stated as a design decision, not an omission. (1) TOOL — a sufficiency probe that, given an unresolved anchor, searches the frozen FR index for any rule between the base vintage and the rule date that touched this section, and returns the candidate set or empty. (2) VERIFICATION — a scoring rule that makes confident wrongness cost more than silence: +1 for a correct call, 0 for a correct abstention, -1 for a confident wrong call. That single choice pins both degenerate policies below the honest floor and it is the cleanest possible answer to the CEO's circularity objection, because the scorer is arithmetic over string equality with no model anywhere. The ablation is a two-cell diagonal: remove the sufficiency probe and STALE_BASE recall goes to chance; remove the restraint rule and the false-defect rate on stale items goes to ~1.0.
proposals.corpus: Same govinfo trio, and the phenomenon is already measured. In my title-31 / March-2024 run, of 57 real quoted-anchor removal instructions checked against the CFR 2023 annual edition, 12.3% had the anchor missing at every normalisation level and a further 12.3% targeted a section not present in that edition at all — roughly a quarter of clean instructions look defective purely because the base is stale. Item construction is mechanical and needs no judgement: hand the agent the year N-2 annual edition where the rule was written against year N-1 plus intervening amendments, and the gold label is STALE_BASE by construction; hand it the correct vintage and gold is EXECUTES or DEFECTIVE from the EDNOTE / correction channels. Both bundles are real, unedited GPO text of the same section, so nothing about the artifact's shape betrays the class.
proposals.licence: Identical and clean: GPO/OFR/NARA, 17 U.S.C. §105, govinfo /bulkdata keyless and not robots-disallowed. One thing to disclose loudly in the README, because it is an intervention on the data rather than a selection: this design requires STRIPPING the <CITA> source-credit element from the shipped section text (see the trivial attack). Stripping a field is a freeze choice, not a text modification, and the surviving text is verbatim GPO — but it must be named as a design decision with its reason, in the same place as the metric, or it reads as tuning.
proposals.primary_metric: Expected score per instruction under the published proper scoring rule (+1 correct / 0 abstain / -1 confident-wrong), normalised to [0,1], with the three-class confusion matrix printed in full and per-class recall reported separately — never a single blended number. Deterministic, stdlib, no model. Chance for a uniform random guesser is 0 under this rule, not 0.333. Secondary: STALE_BASE localisation accuracy (did it name the right missing FR citation), and the abstention rate per class, because an agent that abstains everywhere scores 0 and must be visibly distinguishable from one that is calibrated.
proposals.trivial_attack_and_why_it_fails: **I have to report that the strongest attack WINS on the raw corpus, and that this proposal only survives a stated freeze intervention.** THE ATTACK, ~10 lines: read the section's <CITA> source credit — verbatim format '[71 FR 18612, Apr. 12, 2006, as amended at 87 FR 77478, Dec. 19, 2022]' — take the latest FR date in it, and compare it to the rule's publication date. If the credit stops before the rule, the base is stale. That is close to a perfect classifier for the STALE_BASE class and it needs no model. It is defeated only by removing <CITA> from the shipped text, which is defensible on the merits (the source credit is produced by the codifier AFTER the fact; the drafter reasoning about her own working copy does not have tomorrow's credit) but it is unquestionably an intervention I chose. Once CITA is stripped, distinguishing a stale base from a defective instruction requires reading the intervening rules in the frozen FR index and reasoning about whether one of them plausibly changed the anchored text — which no short script does. Second attack, always-abstain: scores exactly 0 by the scoring rule. Third, always-DEFECTIVE-on-unresolved-anchor: scores negative on the stale class, which is roughly half the set. Both pinned. Verdict: the attack wins on the natural corpus and loses on the frozen one, and that asymmetry is this proposal's central liability — a hostile judge is entitled to ask why the field was removed, and the answer has to be in the README before they ask.
proposals.hard_case: An instruction whose anchor is missing for BOTH reasons at once: an intervening rule changed the surrounding paragraph AND the drafter also mis-transcribed the quoted phrase. Correct behaviour is not a class label, it is a routed human checkpoint with both readings and the paragraph trace — which satisfies ground rules 04 and 05 with one named checkpoint at one named failure mode, rather than a blanket approval gate that reads as compliance theatre. The measured seeds are already in hand: '§ 546.201(a)' as an anchor inside a section the same rule restructures, and ', but are not limited to,' absent from a base that is up to 12 months stale.
proposals.beats_incumbent_because: It is the only one of the three whose primary metric pins BOTH degenerate policies at or below zero rather than at 0.500, so the trivial-solution test is passed by the scoring rule itself rather than by a permutation null — and it is built on a failure mode I measured at ~24.6% of real instructions rather than one I hypothesised. It also occupies the abstention lane, which the strategy brief's live probe found at 0 of 64 visible entries, and it directly instantiates micro1's own published position that restraint is a first-class outcome. Against the incumbent specifically: the incumbent's guard metric caps false-defects at 0.25 as an afterthought; here the false-defect/stale-base confusion IS the task, so the thing the incumbent measures as a side constraint becomes the object under test.
proposals.honest_weakness: It is the weakest of the three and I would rank it third. (1) The 10-line CITA attack wins unless a field is stripped, and the stripping is a choice I made — everything downstream inherits that asterisk. Proposals 1 and 2 have no equivalent. (2) The STALE_BASE class is generated by construction (I decide which vintage to hand over), so the ground truth is only partly externally authored — the incumbent's property-1 claim of zero authored ground truth does not survive here, and pretending otherwise would be exactly the kind of overstatement the kill test caught twice. (3) It overlaps Proposal 1 heavily. Realistically this is not a separate project; it is Proposal 1's fourth case class and its best guard metric. My recommendation is to build Proposal 1 and fold this in as class T, keeping the three-way output and the proper scoring rule, rather than shipping it standalone — unless the H5 ledger-script baseline kills Proposal 1's headline, in which case this framing survives independently because its foreclosure comes from the scoring rule and not from the script's precision.

kills.candidate: Codify — replay the amendment, don't predict it
kills.trivial_attack_result:
I reproduced the rival's pool from scratch on govinfo (byte sizes exact: 5,540,292 / 5,524,321 / 6,040,968 / 6,349,337; title-40 vol5 = 9 clean items, title-42 vol5 = 70 clean / 22 chained — all three numbers reproduce exactly; eCFR and federalregister.gov both 403 as claimed; the §52.2540 chain is verbatim as described). Their TRIVIAL floor holds: identity = 0/9 exact (mean char-sim 0.9204), and my own 20-line designation-keyed block splice = 0/9 (sim 0.8892). No constant, lookup or regex wins.

THE FLOOR IS NOT 0.000. I then wrote the baseline they admit they never built. v1 (~70 lines, one pass, ~1h): 2/9 = 0.222 exact. v2 (~95 lines, one fix round, no tuning on a held-out set): 3/9 = 0.333 exact, mean sim 0.8844. It handles exactly four ops — quoted literal substitution, redesignation prefix relabel, add/revise-block splice from the FR SECTION text, and reserved-range shrink — plus a CFR-hierarchy sort. Their own 0/9 carries a 95% binomial upper bound of 0.283; 0.333 is above it. Files: interp.py (0.222), interp2.py (0.333), in the scratchpad.

WHY IT WINS, MEASURED: the oracle-ceiling table. For all 9 items only 1–2 of the gold's paragraph blocks are absent verbatim from (pre-text ∪ FR text ∪ the edition-Y note), and every single absent block differs from an available one by 0.94–0.997 similarity — i.e. by exactly one transformation the AMDPAR literally names ("(c)"→"(c)(1)"; "(b)(2)(v), except"→"(b)(2)(iii), except"; "(i)-(k) [Reserved]"→"(j)-(k) [Reserved]"). The task is block rearrangement plus four string ops in a fixed sublanguage for which OFR publishes a style manual (1 CFR 21, the Document Drafting Handbook). It is a compiler task, and a compiler wins it. Their own estimate for the serious interpreter was 0.30–0.60, unmeasured; it is now measured at 0.333 for 95 lines in under two hours, and 3 of the 6 misses are one opcode away (52.2070 sim 0.9903, 52.2540 sim 0.9355).

BONUS LEAK: 53.0% of every character inserted into the gold across the 9 items is already printed verbatim inside the 2023 edition XML that is handed to the agent as input, in <EFFDNOTP><REVTXT> pending-amendment blocks. 5 of the 9 items carry one.
kills.fatal_flaw:
THE PURITY-GATE PINCER — the same structure that killed CROSSCheck, rotated 90 degrees. Their guard metric keeps items whose pre→post diff is confined to designations the AMDPARs name. Measured on title-40 vol5: 15 of 24 text-changed sections (62.5%) changed with NO new FR citation at all — four by literally one space or one capital letter (§52.2299 sim 1.0000 yet unequal; §52.2495 one deleted space; §52.2428 one inserted space; §52.2275 'A'→'a' ×2), and two by real amendments the CITA never names (§52.2059 gained a whole paragraph (z); §52.2120 has 41 opcodes). In title-42, 15 of 82 changed sections have a sub-0.05% delta. So: gate tight ⇒ you keep exactly the items whose delta is the instructions' literal effect, which is the set a deterministic interpreter is built to win (script ↑, headroom ↓). Gate loose ⇒ exact-match is unattainable for anything that sees only pre-text + instructions, because the residual is OFR's unpublished editorial act (agent = script = 0). There is no setting that leaves an agent-shaped band. You cannot make the residual hard without making it impossible.

FIVE MORE, ALL MEASURED:
(1) THEIR HARVEST IS CONTAMINATED BY THE ARTIFACT THEY THINK THEY STRIPPED. Nine SECTNOs are duplicated in the 2023 volume — all nine from EFFDNOTP. A last-wins parse gives §52.2540 a 425-char "pre-text" when the real section is 7,249. Five of their nine items (52.2040, 52.2283, 52.2440, 52.2540, 52.2587) are exactly those duplicates, and their showcase hard case is wrong: §52.2356 IS present in the 2023 body (2,387 chars), so "the section does not exist at edition Y" is an artifact of reading the note fragment as the section.
(2) n=9 IS n≈5. §52.2040/§52.2440/§52.2540 carry BYTE-IDENTICAL AMDPARs from one rule; §52.2283/§52.2587 near-identical. My interpreter got 2040 and 2440 together for that reason. Every per-item number is rule-clustered; "70 items" is not 70 trials.
(3) THE 30-POINT ROW IS TWO-THIRDS HOLLOW. TOOL = "an LLM can't re-emit 5–30KB verbatim, so use targeted edits" — that is str_replace_editor / Anthropic's text_editor, shipped 2024, and the ablation is forced precisely because everyone already knows the answer; a strawman with a number on it. MEMORY = an ablation that is "0.000 by construction" is a tautology, not an experiment, and the thing being called memory is `state = apply(state, op)`, a loop accumulator — exactly the component-inflation the PDF names ("Purposeful choices matter more than the number of components"). Only VERIFICATION survives cross-examination. One real capability, one table-stakes tool, one variable → 17/30, not the 26–28 implied.
(4) USER VALUE INVERTS. The gold is the authority's own free, machine-readable output from the same govinfo endpoint the project harvests. A rule package contains amendatory instructions, not codified text; codification is OFR's job and OFR publishes it within days. Willingness to pay ≈ 0 for a machine that guesses what the authority already prints. The incumbent's answer does not exist anywhere at prediction time.
(5) PRIOR ART. "Automatic consolidation of legislative texts with the extraction and application of amendments" is a named, standardised task with a 15-year literature (Akoma Ntoso change management, Springer 2011; AKN4UN "Management of Modifications"; Xcential/Propylon commercial pipelines; legislation.gov.uk) and the eCFR is itself the shipped product of it. Straight into the strategy brief's "solved problems that must not be presented as novel" bucket.
(6) 24h IS OPTIMISTIC BY ~2×. They commit to shipping the interpreter as the loud H5 baseline. It is the largest artifact in the plan and it is the BASELINE, not the solution. Plus 44 FR issues for title-42 (they budgeted 20), GPOTABLE row surgery, purity instrumentation, and an agent arm that has never once been run.

kills.candidate: Codify or Refuse — execution with a restraint class
kills.trivial_attack_result:
TWO attacks, both measured, both beat or tie the metric.
